November 29, 1974 Mr. J. Campbell (LaSalle-Emard-COte Saint-Paul) chairman of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications:
That the second report of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, presented to the House on Thursday, November 21, 1974, be concurred in.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yesterday, in reference to this subject matter, it was indicated that the Chair was in considerable doubt as to the propriety of the report from the procedural point of view. I invited hon. members who wanted to do so to contribute to that subject today. It would be my intention to hear hon. members who wish to make a contribution and probably to reserve whatever judgment I propose to deliver until some time later this week.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Thursday apparently there was procedural difficulty regarding this recommendation brought before the House. We have been able to gather some material that I believe will be helpful to the Chair in reaching a decision. During the consideration of private members' business last Thursday there was an indication that the Chair might be asked to rule at the appropriate time on whether or not the second report of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications could be received. Before such decision is taken I would seek from the Chair permission to make some comments.
It was argued last Thursday that it was beyond the capability of a standing committee to make a report of this nature to the House since its order of reference was only to consider Bill S-ll. The authority cited was Beauchesne's Fourth Edition, citation 304, where it is stated:
(1)	A committee may only consider those matters which have been committed to it by the House.
(2)	A committee is bound by, and not at liberty to depart from, the order of reference.
Beauchesne himself cited his own authority, which was the Fourth Edition of Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure, page 469. It appears that the House may have strayed from the original principle in recent years to the point where it may be useful to quote the original authority in extenso: I believe most hon. members are aware that the two paragraphs I have mentioned go beyond Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure. There are two sentences in this citation which should be considered very closely. The first is:
Consequently, if a bill be referred to a select committee it will not be competent for that committee to go beyond the subject matter of its provisions.
It would appear clear that committees are not restricted to the provisions of a bill but can also consider the subject matter of the provisions of a bill, public or private. Accordingly, committees should indeed be competent to submit to the House recommendations dealing with the subject matter of the provisions of a bill. Should the judgment of the committee be challenged, then it should be through a decision of the House and not a decision of the Chair. The second sentence or part thereof which warrants attention is the following:
No such restrictions apply to committees on private bills ...
There may be some who would argue that this citation finds no application, but the fact is that there appears to be no precedent where the House or Mr. Speaker have refused committees the right to submit to the House reports of the nature of the report now brought before it. Dealing in particular with recommendations submitted by committees in relation to private bills, Bourinot at pages 603-604 reads as follows:
In case the bill is withdrawn or otherwise fails to become law, the fee of $200 is refunded, generally and properly on the recommendation of the committee on the bill. Sometimes the committee will recommend that it be refunded on other grounds:
Because a bill has been rendered necessary by the action of the general legislature. Because the necessity for its passage arose from no fault of the promoter, but from circumstances beyond his control. Because the committee have materially diminished the powers asked for. Because it is not liable to the fee and charges levied on private bills. Because it is a mere amendment to the general act respecting banks and banking. Because a project is of a great public benefit to a locality, because the promoters of the bill have agreed to accept the provisions of a general act passed that session: because it has to a great extent been superseded by the provisions of a public bill. Because a bill

December 3, 1974
Transport and Communications
has been consolidated with another, on which fees are paid, or because it is a mere amendment to a previous act.
The only vehicle available to committees, on a bill for presentation to the House, of such recommendations is a report. The House has consistently received from committees dealing with private bills, reports containing recommendations without challenge. The fact is that if the Chair refuses to seize the House of the second report of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications it would probably be establishing a new rule for which it would be difficult to find a precedent. Should the Chair allow itself to be placed in a position where it would be substituting its judgment for that of a committee on grounds other than procedural grounds? The question is of some importance because there does exist an analogous precedent in recent years, at least as far as procedure is concerned.
It is true that the mode of relieving a company of charges levied under standing orders is different, but that is a matter of judgment to be decided by the House and not a matter of procedure to be decided by the Chair. On May 30, 1967, the House referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, Bill C-104, an act respecting the Bell Telephone Company. On October 20, 1967, the committee submitted to the House the following report:
Your committee has before it Bill C-104, an act respecting the Bell Telephone Company of Canada.
Your committee unanimously recommends that the capital stock charges in the amount of $150,400 collected and paid to the Receiver General of Canada, and deposited in the Consolidated Revenue Fund in the course of the past session (1966-67), by the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, be applied to the capital stock charges levied at this session.
The said report was concurred in on October 24, 1967. The Chair then had no objection whatsoever to the moving of a motion for concurrence in the said report. It is therefore difficult to understand why any objection should be raised to a motion for concurrence in a similar report at this time. The Chair is now being asked to rule out of order what the House declared in order only a few years back. Should the Chair decide that committees cannot submit recommendations in any form to the House in connection with their consideration of bills, then there will undoubtedly arise problems of a practical nature. May I quote, as one example, the report submitted by the Standing Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines on March 24, 1960, which was concurred in by the House on the same day:
Your committee reported this day Bill S-16, an act to incorporate Matador Pipe Line Company, Ltd., as its fourth report.
Clause 3 of the bill provides for capital stock of one hundred thousand common shares without nominal or par value.
Your committee recommends that, for taxing purposes under Standing Order 94, each common share shall be deemed to be worth one dollar.
By unanimous consent, on motion of Mr. Howe, seconded by Mr. Baldwin, the said report was concurred in.
If committees are not permitted to report recommendations to the House, then in such cases there can be no application of the provisions of Standing Order 91 inasmuch as there would be left no vehicle whereby the committee could ask the House to agree to an evaluation of shares. The same would be true of Standing Order 105.

May I assure you, Mr. Speaker, and the House that the committee, in ordering the presentation of its second report to the House acted in good faith and within the four corners of parliamentary tradition. If Your Honour decides to take under advisement the objections raised, then may I suggest that the following points be considered. First, there is little basis for the contention that committees charged with the consideration of a bill cannot submit recommendations to the House. Second, dealing with private bills specifically, there would appear to be no precedent where a committee report was ruled out of order on the grounds that the bill was the order of reference and recommendations could not be received. Third, the report submitted to the House by the committee is procedurally consistent with each and every report of the same nature submitted by this or any other committee in the past. It has not been brought to the attention of the Chair that any such report was ever ruled out or order, and the Chair might not wish to impose upon committees conditions which the House itself did not impose either through its Standing Orders or its decisions.
Fourth, a decision to deny committees considering bills, public or private, the right to submit from time to time reports containing recommendations would necessarily entail far reaching consequences in several areas: For instance, where a committee submits that a bill be divided, that a witness has refused to appear, that the order of reference should be expanded, that the bill should more properly be considered by another committee, that the committee be allowed to travel, etc.
In conclusion, the committee which honoured me by electing me its chairman has taken a unanimous decision which it hopes will be submittted to the judgment of the House. Decisions of the Chair are not subject to appeal, and should the decision of the Chair be that the report of the committee is out of order there would be no opportunity left for the members of the committee to justify, in parliament, their position. The committee felt that it was acting within its capability, competence and responsibility and hopes that its decision will be concurred in by the House.
I would respectfully request that the motion be put, but if there are misgivings it would be my suggestion that all the matters raised today in this respect be referred for immediate consideration either to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization or to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills and Standing Orders.

speakeroldname: Mr. John M. Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I at the outset indicate my support for the position which the committee has taken in this report, namely, that the company concerned should not have to pay the very extravagant fee which is apparently required in this case. However, there is a procedural point of some importance here. It concerns the powers of parliamentary committees to make representations to the House of Commons. Your Honour will recall that your predecessor, Mr. Speaker Lamoureux, on June 18, 1973 delivered a ruling on the nature and the ability of a committee to make a report on the estimate. Taking that as the beginning, I submit that the restriction on a committee to make reports on bills
December 3, 1974

referred to it is equally restrictive and obligatory, and that the committee may report only on a bill and amendments thereon. I do not think it necessary to quote the report of the standing committee or the reference. I think these are easily found.
However, I want to deal with House of Commons Standing Order 65(8) which reads as follows:
Standing committees shall be severally empowered to examine and enquire into all such matters as may be referred to them by the House, and, to report from time to time, and, except when the House otherwise orders, to send for persons, papers and records .. .
The point is that the matter of the fee in Bill S-ll, according to the reference on Thursday, November 7, was not referred to the committee and is not encompassed in the reference that was made to that committee. What was referred to the committee was Bill S-ll which the committee must report with or without amendment to the House of Commons. Beauchesne's Fourth Edition, citation 304(1) at page 244 reads:
A committee can only consider those matters which have been committed to it by the House.
Citation 304(2) clearly states, and I quote:
A committee is bound by, and is not at liberty to depart from, the order of reference. In the case of a Select Committee upon a Bill, the Bill committed to it is itself the order of reference to the Committee, who must report it with or without amendment to the House.
May's eighteenth edition at page 620 makes the following point:
A select committee, like a Committee of the whole House, possesses no authority except that which it derives by delegation from the House by which it is appointed. When a select committee is appointed to consider or inquire into a matter, the scope of its deliberations or inquiries is defined by the order by which the committee is appointed (termed the order of reference), and the deliberations or inquiries of the committee must be confined within the limits of the order of reference. But when a bill is committed, or referred, to a select committee, the bill is itself the order of reference, and the inquiries and deliberations of the committee must be confined to the bill and amendments relevant to the subject-matter thereof.
What the House might wish to do concerning the fee paid by British Columbia Telephone Company is a totally separate issue from Bill S-ll. In view of the fact that Bill C-29 will apparently standardize the fees paid by companies seeking to enlarge their capitalization, the House may wish to consider bringing its Standing Order fee provisions into line with the new legislation or it may wish to order the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications or the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills and Standing Orders to consider the question of the fee to be paid, or not paid, by British Columbia Telephone Company. Beauchesne, citation 304(3) at page 244 reads:
When it has been thought desirable to do so, the House has enlarged the order of reference by means of an instruction or in the case of a Select Committee upon a Bill by the committal to it of another Bill. Mandatory instructions have also been given to Select Committees restricting the limits of their powers or prescribing the course of their proceedings, or directing the committee to make a special report upon certain matters.
(4) Sometimes a committee may have to obtain leave from the House to make a special report when its order of reference is limited in scope.
Transport and Communications
Means exist, therefore, under the rules of the House to allow the committee to consider, and make recommendations on, the fee to be paid in connection with Bill S-ll. However, such means do not now exist under the committee's present order of reference with application to Bill S-ll and any recommendation other than reporting the bill with or without amendments is out of order.
The important thing here is the nature of the reference and the fact that in commenting on the fee payable the committee exceeded its order of reference. The normal procedure of the House of Commons is that a committee has the power to amend a bill, by which means it expresses its opinion on the bill. Such a report, including an amendment, is, in effect, a report to the House of Commons that a substantive change is necessary. But the authorities do not contemplate at any point the possibility of a committee making extraneous reports or commentaries on legislation referred to it in the form of a bill.
I think Your Honour must find, taking into consideration the arguments I have advanced, and the direction your predecessor has provided, that this report is out of order.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
As I see it, Mr. Speaker, the problem inherent in the procedural point raised regarding this report is referable to section 16 of the Financial Administration Act. While I am in considerable sympathy with the remarks made by the learned chairman of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communication, I should like to call the attention of the House to an interesting reference by a former Auditor General, Mr. Watson Sellar, in an audit office guide which he wrote for the instruction of Treasury Board officers in 1958. On page 24 of this publication, he mentioned a situation which arose in 1929 when motions to remit funds for private bills withdrawn were, for the first time, rejected by the Speaker whose explanation was:
It is essentially contrary to section 35 of the Consolidated Revenue Act (now section 16 of the Financial Administration Act) which stipulates that any fees received by the officers of the House shall be deposited at the bank, when they become the property of the Receiver General of Canada. To remit such fees would require an estimate from the Minister of Finance.
This was reported in Hansard of June 14, 1929, at page 3762. The Speaker's ruling was not, of course, binding on the Senate, so a degree of inconsistency existed in practice until the act was amended.
It seems obvious that the moment the funds were paid by the B.C. Telephone Company they became the property of the Receiver General of Canada and should have been, and likely were, deposited in the Consolidated Revenue Fund by the Chief Clerk of Committees.
It would therefore seem there would be little point at this time in sending a reference to the committee instructing it to deal with the question of the funds, should such action be contemplated, if only because the funds are not there any more; the only way to have them retrieved, if, in fact, it is proper to do so, would be pursuant to section 16 of the Financial Administration Act which is entirely within the discretion of the Minister of Finance. So, regardless of what may happen with regard to Bill C-29, the Canada Business Corporations Act, discretion remains

December 3, 1974
Transport and Communications
with the Minister of Finance to take whatever action he deems to be equitable in the circumstances.
This question is causing considerable concern because of the size of the fee and the relevance it might have to telephone rates in British Columbia. While I am all for seeing the powers of committees preserved and, if possible, extended, I have grave doubts as to the relevance of this recommendation. We are dealing here with a delicate matter related to the responsibilities placed upon some of the officers of the House in connection with fees of this type.

In answer to a question asked a few days ago, the minister indicated that grain inspectors had the right to strike and he expressed the hope that an agreement would be reached by normal means. Is the minister now in a position to announce that indeed such an agreement has been reached?

subtopic: GRAIN INSPECTORS STRIKE-ADEQUACY OF SUPPLIES IN EASTERN CANADA THIS WINTER

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: GRAIN INSPECTORS STRIKE-ADEQUACY OF SUPPLIES IN EASTERN CANADA THIS WINTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a further question for the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, but perhaps the Prime Minister can give me the information. In view of the strike and the absence of any report of a concrete nature from the President of the Treasury Board, and in view of reports abroad that this means a shortage of grain in the east for milling and other purposes, can the Prime Minister tell the House whether his government has had an examination of inventories conducted and that he can assure the House there will be sufficient grain in eastern Canada this winter to meet the needs both for human and animal consumption?

subtopic: GRAIN INSPECTORS STRIKE-ADEQUACY OF SUPPLIES IN EASTERN CANADA THIS WINTER

Mr. Speaker, of course this matter deeply concerns the government, and the minister in particular. We discussed it this morning, he and I, and we will continue to do so during the course of the day. As far as the exact inventory to
Oral Questions
which the Leader of the Opposition referred, it is obvious that that depends on the assumptions considered, namely whether the strike will last any length of time or not.

subtopic: GRAIN INSPECTORS STRIKE-ADEQUACY OF SUPPLIES IN EASTERN CANADA THIS WINTER

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the President of the Treasury Board and it arises out of the fact that as of midnight last night there were approximately 80 oceangoing vessels above the port of St. Lambert and 63 above Port Waller, all of which must be out of the Seaway system by two weeks from today.
In view of this fact that there are currently numerous ocean vessels in the Seaway system capable of transporting grain to eastern terminals before the closure of the system, can the minister assure the House that these vessels will in fact be utilized to alleviate the supply situation in eastern Canada, and that they will not be allowed to leave the system empty of grain cargo?

It is estimated that a ship is capable of carrying up to one million bushels of grain per run, while a boxcar can transport only 2,500 to 3,000 bushels. subsubtopic: AUTOMOBILES-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO DEAL WITH FURTHER LAY-OFFS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. In view of the fact that General Motors Corporation of Canada announced there would be 2,095 employees laid off by that company in the coming weeks, bringing the total number of lay-offs in the automotive industry somewhere in excess of 9,000, I should like to ask the minister if he has been in touch recently with the corporations in Canada to find out what their plans are for the coming weeks and whether he would tell us what plans his government has to deal with the anticipated increase in lay-offs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECTED TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext:
That this House regrets that the Government neglected to make all those who reached the age of 60, as well as their spouses although such spouses may not have reached pensionable age, eligible for the Old Age Pension.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion I am moving in the name of my colleagues of the Social Credit Party of Canada stems from the numerous letters and communications we receive from our constituents, claiming that pensionable age be possible at 60, with an appropriate pension, and that the spouse of a person eligible for old age pension be equally eligible for that pension, as I have been requesting in this House since 1966.
I can hardly believe, Mr. Speaker, that we on this side of the House are the only members receiving such requests from the voters we represent, and I am certain that other members receive the same. Yet, the government is in no hurry to answer the requests of these people. The leader of the liberal party of Canada did promise during the last election campaign that the wife whose husband has reached 65 would be entitled to the old age pension. But we are still far from allowing early retirement at a reasonable age in our modern times when the production of goods and services is increasingly easy.
As soon as the leader of the liberal party resumed his office of Prime Minister, he made a step backwards and we heard in the speech from the Throne that the wife or the spouse will have to wait until October of 1975 at least to see that promise carried out. And yet while he was in Trois-Rivieres, the leader of the liberal party promised that the 60 to 65 year-old wife would receive a pension as soon as the liberal party was reelected. At that time, there is no doubt that many women of that age believed that promise and decided to vote for the Liberals. I would not be surprised that many of them kissed him for that promise. However, they will have to wait for a year and a half after the federal election to see that promise fulfilled. That is the reason why we are blaming the government for not having taken at the beginning of this session the necessary action for the enacting of such legislation and for this government to acknowledge the services those people rendered their country.
With the developments in all types of industries, it seems to me that 42 years of assiduous work are enough to have done one's duty towards society.
The figures of Statistics Canada show that in 1972 the life expectancy was 69.3 years for men and 76.3 years for women. Under the present Old Age Security Act, this

means that a woman has a life expectancy of only 11 years when she reaches retirement age. As for men, they have a life expectancy of only four years when they reach retirement age.
After working hard for more than forty years, men and women should be able to do what they like in complete financial security.
Lowering the eligibility age to 60 for those who wish it would not mean that these people would have to remain inactive. They will be able to render many other services to their country and to their community without being forced to do so. They would be happier.
It is not the first time that we request this in the House. We have done so several times before, and I realize that we are getting more and more support, especially from this side of the House, and that a few government members agree with me but do not dare say so. They say that because of party policy, of government solidarity, the part does not want this change. We shall probably hear the same old objections: "It would cost too much money." Of course, if we think only in terms of dollars or of the taxation capacity, we may be reluctant to accept this proposal but we should see the facts as they really are.
If people aged 60 to 65 agreed to retire at 60, would this weaken the national production rate in Canada? Do we not have a whole army of young people with a college or university education who are waiting only for an employment offer to put their talents to use, to earn their living honourably and to give their services to their country to develop it and serve it? Did we not penalize farmers because they were producing too much?
There has been of late much publicity about the food destroyed. No way could be found sell them, let alone eat them. Industry is slowing down almost everywhere, if not at a standstill, so it is unthinkable not to allow people, men and women, to retire at age 60.
Only yesterday a 65-year-old man told me that because of ill health he had to cease working at 60. Great numbers of people are also worn out or ill well before the present retirement age.
I put this motion forward because I believe the Canadian government can lower retirement age to 60 without upsetting anything.
I am also seeking that old age security pension be paid to the pensioner's spouse as soon as the former reaches retirement age. This is also very important and should be considered now by the government.
Madam Speaker, I have been regularly putting forward a motion of this kind since 1966, the first member I believe to do so. Opposition members supported me, Liberal members spoke against it. But older people, and even the young I meet, all favour such an amendment to the Old Age Security Act. It is at their request that I have caused this motion to appear under my name on the order paper.
When only one of the spouses receives the old age security pension, the income of the couple becomes insufficient and the wife must, most of the times, resort to welfare. In Quebec, I assure you, Madam Speaker, that it is often disheartening for these people to appeal to officials for their living.
December 3, 1974

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECTED TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext: It is a disgrace!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECTED TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext:
Those officials, on the orders of the provincial government dole out the allowances in driblets. We know that the federal government has geared old age security pensions to the cost of living. Now, I remember the case of a couple in my constituency; the husband is eligible for old age security pension. Recently, I have received a letter whose main point I would like to have entered into the record. It has been sent to me by a citizen of Taschereau, in my riding, and she acquaints me of the situation.
In October, she writes, my husband received $192.80 as an old age security allowance, plus $43.72 from the Quebec Pension Plan; I, his wife, have received $20 from the welfare, which makes a total amount of $256.52 for the month.
This month, that is in November, she says, in spite of their saying that my husband is going to receive much more, here are the facts: old age security pension, $199.10; QPP, $43.72; welfare, $13; that is to say 70c. less, because of the increase in the old age security allowance.
Then, on the whole, this couple has 70c. less than they received before the increase. Here is indeed a strange increase in income for the aged.
So for the months of October, November and December, this couple received a little less than before. To the government of Quebec, inflation is not a problem, but it is nevertheless true that this couple and many others in the same situation are hit very hard, even harder than those with higher incomes.
The National Council of Welfare, in its report on the situation of the low income consumer on the Canadian market, published in April 1974, explained how families with low incomes have to spend more for food, for example, than families with incomes superior to the average.
We are given the example of a family whose annual income is $3,000 or less and 27.9 per cent of this must be spent on food while a family whose income is $15,000 or more only spends 13.4 per cent. The same goes for housing, clothing and all of life's necessities.
Statistics Canada tell us that the price index went from 100 in 1961 to 188.4 in June 1974 for food; 165.5 for housing;
152.0	for clothing; 169.3 for personal care and hygiene; 151.2 for public transport and 156.9 for recreation, training and reading. That goes to show that the galloping inflation we have known especially from 1968 to 1973 has become dizzying in 1973 and 1974 and we are now being told it will be a knockout in 1975 and it is a cause of concern and hardship for the families and old people in the low income bracket.
That is why the government must come to an agreement with the provincial governments so that this law can be modified to reflect the motion I have moved.
There is also another point on which I want to bring the attention of the government and my colleagues in this House, even though the motion does not deal with it, and it is the guaranteed minimum income supplement that goes with the old age security pension. The pension should be paid in full without any means test because otherwise, as is the case now, those who have a job-however temporary-are being penalized. Those who have a few savings
Old Age Pensions
or who paid into a retirement annuity in a private business are being penalized. Since 1966, a legislation forces them to do without part of their salary which is paid into a federal or provincial pension plan, and when they reach the age of retirement, they lose part of the guaranteed income supplement. That is an injustice for those who worked, who paid taxes, who managed to make good use of their savings. Those who did not work half the time, who "invested" their money in taverns, are entitled to everything. A system like that does not make sense.
Let us do away with the tests, let us all recognize that Canadians are entitled to their pensions as soon as they reach 60, and that both husband and wife are entitled to it. That is what we are asking for on behalf of Canadians, and to refuse it to them is not to believe in the wealth of this country, nor in the capacity of our young people to produce goods and services in large quantity as we have already done.
Madam Speaker, I ask the government and government members to consider that motion and respond to it in an objective and above all affirmative way. As I said at the outset, this is not the first time we make that request. I know we must hit the nail several times to get it in but the government must understand that the head of the nail is now at ground level and it is time to get it over with. I am sure my colleagues will put forward other arguments in support of that motion, and I hope that before this day is over the government will show flexibility, and that it will introduce before Christmas the necessary bill to meet the wishes of the Canadian people.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECTED TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the motion before us is a very appealing one and I congratulate its mover. Indeed, I congratulate the members of his group generally. I have noted that time after time they have brought forward measures which they consider in the interests of that very important part of the national constituency, the aged and the needy. I think it behooves us as serious legislators-I have said this many times in my public career-to take the attitude at all times that the government must exhibit the greatest care toward those who most need care.
I am not an advocate of the fiscal theories of the Social Credit group, and even if I understood them I do not think I would be, but I nevertheless commend them for being interested in and articulating on behalf of the poor and the elderly people of this country. It is we in this House who must speak for these constituents. We must vote for measures to help them and use the state to help ameliorate the ravages of raging inflation. As I say, I commend the mover of this motion. I have very much sympathy for the thrust of the motion. I think the day will come-and it will not be too far removed from today-when we will be looking at the age of 60 as we now look at the age of 65, and as we once looked at the age of 70, as the time when we put into operation what we now call, and what may some day be changed, our old age security system. I am not terribly old, though I may look it, but I well remember occasions when people have said, "You can't lower the retirement age from

70 to 65 because you will ruin the whole country. You have no idea how much it will cost".
Yet we have survived this de-escalation. The country still exists. It is not as healthy as it would be if we were well governed. But society has not been blown asunder. However, we must never forget that there is far too much poverty in this land. Just because we hear this said day in and day out is no reason for resting content. We are told that one in four Canadians lives on or below the poverty line-and I can assure hon. members it is not gracious living. I know that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) was very callous and cool the other day when I referred to the message of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) to the old age pensioners, namely, that they save money by eating stale bread, peanut butter and skim milk powder. speechtext:
little reckless. If in ten years time, when I would be 65, I were able to convince a 19-year old girl to run the risk of living with me, she would become an old age security recipient for goodness knows how long. She might earn her living if she were living with me. However, I think we must be realistic. My colleague wonders whether I am bragging or complaining, and I will not tell him which it is.
When my party was appealing for public support we said honestly and squarely what we would do. We gave the age of 55. I think the government's announced age-and I wish it would bring in the legislation-of 60 is less realistic than ours. Since the government took the idea from us, I think it should take over the age that we proposed and we would support it. But I cannot honestly go so far as saying that age is immaterial. I know that the motto amor vincit omnia really still prevails, but I do not think we could seriously legislate that age does not matter.
There are two other aspects of this matter with which I should like to deal before I sit down. I know the minister is aware of this as we on this side of the House are aware of it. When we look into the area of considering the spouse who is not of qualified age we immediately have many thoughtful Canadians who ask-and they are right-is it not more likely that the widowed person will be in far greater need than the one who still has a spouse? So when you take that first step-and it is a good one and I am with the members of the Social Credit Party although I think the age figure is too low-then you are open to even greater sensitivity about the people who have been widowed.
One woman wrote to me and said, "I am 63 and my husband is 69. When the government puts the bill through, if I lose my husband in a year's time, what happens? Am I taken off the rolls just when I need help more?" That is another thing we must look at. What do we do about the spouse under 65 who qualifies through marriage-marriage is a partnership and a lot of other things-and what happens when someone is widowed and is still too young to qualify for OAS? I find, as I am sure the minister and the mover of this motion find, that this general question opens many avenues down which we must move with great care.
I do not wish to take all the time available to me, but I reiterate my commendation of the mover of this motion. I express to him my general sympathy for it. However, I have tried to underline with a little realism some of the economic responsibilities this expression of compassion would entail. But I congratulate him for drawing our attention to just the kind of problem that serious legislators should never lose sight of.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECTED TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) in commending the hon. member for.Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) and his party on the subject they have placed before the House of Commons on this allotted day. Any motion dealing with pensioners and calling for an improvement in the position of pensioners has my immediate support, even though I might want to change some of the details in a motion such as the one placed before us. The hon. member for Abitibi was quite correct- I can certainly confirm it-that one of the ways to win
Old Age Pensions
improvements for old age pensioners is to keep at the issue day in and day out, week in and week out, year in and year out and decade in and decade out. The encouraging thing is that by keeping at it we do make considerable
progress.
I agree with the previous speaker that there are other issues that are of concern in the social security field. The hon. member mentioned several groups, such as the disabled and the blind. He mentioned persons on private pensions, and I would add those on government annuities, and so on. One must also think of those who are in that grey area where they are employed and therefore cannot qualify for social assistance but are not earning enough to have a decent standard of living. We sometimes refer to them as the working poor. It certainly is a fact that the area of social security is an important one in which, even with all that we have done, there is a great deal yet to do. Yet it seems to me it is no excuse for not doing something about old age pensions at age 60 to say that there are other things that should be done which the government is not doing anyway.
Therefore, I welcome this motion with its particular emphasis. I confess that in my view there is a bit of confusion in the motion and a bit of confusion in the mind of the hon. member for Abitibi as to whether what is being pressed is a program for pensions at 60 or a program under which the spouse will receive the pension no matter what the age of the spouse, provided the other spouse qualifies for the pension. In my view, the best way to deal with the matter of providing an income for the younger spouse of a pensioner is to lower the pension age.
As the hon. member for Hillsborough pointed out, if and when the government brings in its bill on pensions for spouses between the ages of 60 and 65, provided the other spouse is over 65, we will immediately be deluged with letters from widows, spinsters, widowers and bachelors in that same age bracket who will ask, "If it is possible to provide old age pensions to some people who are between 60 and 65, why not to the rest of us?" I urge that the way some of us have been proposing for a long time is really the way to cope with this problem. In fact, I have it on the order paper in my private member's motion No. 39 which calls for the eligible age under both the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan to be lowered to 60, with the proviso that between 60 and 65 pensions under those two pieces of legislation should be paid only to those who are out of the labour market. That would include, in most cases, spouses who are younger than the person who is already on the pension and all wives between 60 and 65 who are not in the labour market. It seems to me that this is a better way to do it, because at the same time you are making it possible for widows, spinsters, widowers and bachelors in that age bracket to get the pension if, as I say, they are out of the labour market.
That is why I welcome the motion this afternoon. Its terms are broad enough to allow us to talk about any aspect of social security or pension policy. Indeed, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) can tell us about his orange paper and about the discussions he is having with the provinces. The field is as wide as you can possibly imagine. But no matter how wide the

field is, there are times when one should concentrate on a particular point or two. In my view, what is now urgent in the pension field is that we concentrate on two things: one is to get the voluntary pension age down to 60, and the other is to get the basic amount paid under the Old Age Security Act up to $200 a month without a means test of any kind.
With regard to the lowering of the pension age to 60, as I have already said, my view is that the time has not yet come to make it universal at 60 the way it is now at 65, but I insist that the time has come when the pension should be available at 60 to those who are off the labour market. That would include persons like wives, for example, who have not been in the labour market. It would also include those who are working but are prepared to retire.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECTED TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext: All wives?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECTED TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext:
All wives who are out of the labour market and all husbands out of the labour market, too. I was not indulging in any discrimination when I referred to wives rather than spouses in that context. I was talking about wives who are not in the labour market, and in my view they would be covered by the kind of definition that I suggest. I have no idea how many persons would drop out of the labour market in that age bracket, but I expect it would be several hundred thousand and that this would have an immediate effect on the unemployment situation by opening up a great many jobs for younger persons.
But I am concerned not only for the spouses, the persons who are at home and who are out of the labour market, but about a large number of individuals, working men and women. However, I refer more to working men, for a reason I shall give in a moment, who find the rat race of modern industrial activity a little hard to take over an extended period of time. We had a discussion a few days ago on a bill having to do with the fighting of elections and I had occasion to refer to my favourite method of campaigning at election time, which is to turn up early at shop gates and plant gates in the whole area of greater Winnipeg and to meet a great many working men and women as they are going into those plants.
In the last election, as in the previous ones, the question that was put to me most often, especially by the men who were going into the CPR shops, the CNR shops, Dominion Bridge, Manitoba Bridge, packing plants and so on, was, "When are you going to get the pension age down to 60?" Some of the men who put that question to me appeared, in the grey light of the early morning, older than I am-and around here I am supposed to look old. Some of these men who are asking me for the pensionable age to be lowered to 60 appeared to me to be 63 or 65 already, and in instance after instance I had these men say to me, "I am 57" or "I am 58." The fact is that the rat race of that kind of life is just too hard and I think that they have the right, having gone to work at the age of 25 or even younger or later than that, by the time they are 60, if they want to leave that kind of activity and enjoy the benefits of our social legislation, including in particular old age security and the Canada Pension Plan, to do so.
I know all the arguments that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has. If he has any new ones, I will be

delighted to hear them. But he talks about other needs that must be met and the things that he is working on under the aegis of his orange paper, which is a good paper that I like very much. He may even throw at me the question, "What about millionaires between the age of 60 and 65 who are out of the labour market?" There are so few of them that they do not worry me very much. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) could take care of them. I doubt that the Minister of National Health and Welfare will throw that argument at me today after what the Minister of Finance did in his budget. He did not show greater concern for pensioners who are at the lower end of the scale. He showed greater concern for the wealthy. He provided an improvement for the 30 per cent or 40 per cent of pensioners at the top, but he provided nothing for the 55 per cent, 60 per cent or 65 per cent of pensioners at the bottom of the pension income scale.
I say to the minister that it is time for him to get off this kick that there is something wrong with my head-on program for pensions at 60. He should become more aware of the experience in this modern industrial society and realize that this is one of the campaigns that he should be on as well. The campaign to get the pension age down to 60, not on a means test basis or welfare basis but on a voluntary basis. Let those who want to keep on working- some of us may want to go on for a long time-do so, but let those who feel they have had all they can take, or those who are in need, have the opportunity, without any means test, meeting only the test of being out of the labour market, to get their full Canada Pension Plan and their full old age security pension at the age of 60.
Because this motion today gives those of us who feel this way the opportunity to press this point, I am very grateful to my friends in the Social Credit Party for having made it the subject of this allotted opposition day. One of the arguments that we get is that it cannot be done, that it would upset our economy, it would cost a great many dollars and, where is the money coming from? Well, I have not been here through the whole history of pensions, but I was reading and following what was going on back in the middle 1920s and I have been here for most of the changes that have taken place. I simply have to say that that has been the argument every time. When J. S. Woodsworth stood in this House and called for a pension of $20 a month payable at age 70, he was told by the minister of finance of that day that the country could not afford it. When it got over to the other place, they used the argument that it would bankrupt the country to pay $20 pensions to our old people. They said it would not be good for older people to have this kind of hand-out from the state.
Mr. Speaker, we got the pension started in the middle twenties. In January, 1927, It became effective at $20 a month at age 70, with a severe means test. When I came here in the early forties it was still that pension. I can remember that when I was arguing that it should be raised from $20 to $30 and the age brought down to 65, with the means test removed, I was told by the older men of that day that I had some good ideas but it could not be done. Well, Mr. Speaker, we have succeeded in getting the pension raised from $20 a month to almost $120 as a basic
December 3, 1974

pension, without a test of any kind, and we have had the age reduced to 65. That is one of the most recent instances of something being done that they said could not be done. The day finally came when Mr. Pearson and his government realized they could reduce the age a year at a time from 70 to 65.
More recently we were told that we could not escalate the old age pension by more than 2 per cent per year. During the days of the minority government, however, we got that 2 per cent ceiling removed and pensions now escalate according to the statistical increase in the cost of living. I shall have something to say-time does not permit me to go into it now-about the way it is always calculated behind the time when it is needed, and so on. The point I am making is that all the things we are now doing in terms of pensions are things we were told earlier could not be done. Let us not have any more of the suggestion that pensions cannot be lowered to age 60. Let us put it down to 64 now, 63 next year, and so on. Other improvements have been won, and this improvement can also be won. In my view, it is a matter of great urgency.
In a moment I shall indicate one of the reasons I am glad my friends put this subject down today. I would rather we had debated my motion, which I think is more comprehensive, but the luck of the draw was against me. I drew position No. 39 with my private member's motion, so the chances of its being reached are not good. I am therefore glad to have this debate today because we are a few months ahead of the day when the Minister of National Health and Welfare will bring in his bill on pensions for spouses where those spouses are between 60 and 65 and where the other spouse is a pensioner. It has the proviso, however, that the younger person is to get a pension only on the basis of an income test. I hope the minister will give me credit for the struggle to say "income test". As far as I am concerned, it is still a "means" test, but I know he is sensitive about the word.
The reason I am glad to have this debate today is that it gives us a chance to plead with the minister to go further with that bill. During the election campaign, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced the program of pensions for spouses he said it would create problems. He referred to spinsters, widows and other persons and said it had to be a tentative program. I say to him that the government will have a great deal of trouble over a program as limited as the one that is proposed, and they should think about it now. The bill that has been promised for pensions only for spouses between 60 and 65, on an income test, should be transformed into a program that meets the needs of today. That is, Mr. Speaker, a program of pensions at 60 for those not in the labour market. This should apply both to old age security and the Canada Pension Plan, and the time for this is now.

speakeroldname: Miss Coline Campbell (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECTED TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I speak on behalf of the government against the motion proposed by the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) who has advocated that the old age security pension be given to any person who has reached the age of 60, as well as to the spouse even if the spouse has not reached pensionable age. The question is not really as simple as the Credit Social would like it to appear and it
Old Age Pensions
must be looked at from an altoghether different aspect than just lowering the age to 60 in order to obtain the old age security. We must ask the question, "How well can all the other needs and the needs of people who are not old be given the attention they deserve?" This question becomes important if we allow spending to increase income maintenance for the elderly only.
I should like to remind hon. members that the elderly are being well taken care of by the government. I will leave it to other speakers on behalf of the government to speak of the benefits available to the elderly. However, I would point out that government programs are already available for any person who becomes sick and is not able to work prior to age 65. Such persons would draw benefits under the Canada Pension Plan already in existence, benefits under the assistance available to veterans, or from the Canada Assistance Plan.
Mr. Speaker, this motion is asking the government to set a new age for retirement. Such a measure would entail a great deal of expenditure by the government, expenditure which is needed in other areas.
The question arises: Are we certain that this area requires new action right now by the government? Is it really our most pressing social problem? Because if implemented, it probably would absorb for some time to come a lot of the additional tax resources available to the government. The cost of such a proposal has been estimated at almost $l2/3 billion of net additional expenditure. Again, Mr. Speaker, one must look at the needs of all the Canadian people and at the government's responsibility to fulfil those needs. It is proper for the government to think in terms of those who are retired, and they have put forth some fine plans to appeal to that age group, such as New Horizons, the Canada Pension Plan and its recent amendments which come into effect January 1, 1975, as well as senior citizens' housing and homes for persons unable to take care of themselves. As well, there is the increase every three months in the OAS and the GIS.
But there are in our society many other people with needs which are attended to by the government of Canada. They must also be looked at in the perspective of benefits provided by the government in terms of the elderly. What are these needs? There are problems other than social security, such as pollution abatement, energy resource development, transportation and problems in our north, to mention a few, which are applicable across Canada. There are social problems apart from income security. They are mainly health care, housing, native development and daycare. These are just some of the areas to which the government must direct its attention and try to meet the needs that exist.
Also, there are the investment programs designed to give Canadians income security from their own employment. Such programs consist of economic development, manpower training and regional expansion programs of all varieties. These programs cry for greater attention, and should have the attention of the government in order that their greater development may come about because they benefit so many Canadians. Apart from considering where government money should be spent, we must remember that many people who are not old rely on the government for income support. These people include the disabled, the

December 3, 1974
Old Age Pensions
physically or mentally handicapped, mothers on their own caring for children, veterans, and foster parents caring for unwanted children. All these people must be encompassed in a program which considers their needs. The question is, how do their needs stand in relation to the need to retire people at age 60, because many people 60 years old can and do earn an income?
Finally, there are also those whose unemployment insurance benefits are inadequate to meet their needs, and there are people in Canada who must be given a supplement of some type in order that they may maintain a minimum standard of earnings. The government has directed itself to the problem of these people and of others as evidenced in the review made in the orange paper, the Working Paper on Social Security tabled in the House in 1973 by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde).
There are a number of questions which should be asked about the desirability of implementing this proposed program as opposed to making improvements to other government programs, for it is impossible to move in all fields simultaneously without bankrupting the Canadian public. Again, one must balance the question of providing earlier pensions against providing more adequately for the needs of non-senior citizens who are unable to support themselves, such as the physically handicapped, the mentally retarded, and one-spouse families. To demonstrate the existing disparity between the income support available to senior citizens and that available to people who are unable to work, it should be noted that in all but one instance- that of the single person rate in Newfoundland-OAS and GIS guarantee levels for single persons and married couples above the rates paid by the provinces for single persons and couples on welfare. Taking the situation in July of this year, OAS and GIS provided $2,306 a year for a single person and $4,400 for a married couple. At the same time, Ontario, New Brunswick and British Columbia, to give just three examples, each had a maximum assistance rate which was below $2,000 a year for a single person. Some figures applying to a married couple are as follows: in British Columbia, $3,240; in Nova Scotia, $3,072.
What about the priority of rehabilitation programs whose aims are helping people who might otherwise rely on welfare to regain or retain their ability to support themselves and their families? These include activities aimed at the vocational rehabilitation of the disabled as well as many programs mounted by the Department of Manpower to assist people with employment difficulties. These programs involve training, mobility, job placement and job creation. They also include many measures aimed at stimulating economic expansion in less developed regions, including native communities. In general, then, the question is this: Given the tremendous amount of new spending which this measure proposed by the Social Credit Party would require, how will the other needs, particularly the individual needs of people not between 60 and 64 years of age, be met?
I remind hon. members, Mr. Speaker, that the federal and provincial ministers of welfare decided in April, 1973, to launch a comprehensive review of the entire Canadian social security system. The objective of the review was to

analyse the system as a whole, not just piece by piece on an ad hoc basis, in order to implement on an integrated basis major reforms urgently needed in all areas. The review was subsequently endorsed by the Canadian first minister's conference. Through this review, the needs of Canadians of all ages will be examined as a whole. The review will investigate the condition of single as well as married people-that is, of both men and women-workers, people who do not work, and people who could work but cannot secure a job, bread-winners and dependants, people who manage on their own and people who need institutional care. It will investigate the condition of people across Canada in cities, towns and rural areas.
Introducing ad hoc measures to help only one area of need on the basis of consideration of one group of our population only, and moving unilaterally on behalf of only one level of government would certainly run counter to the spirit of the review, of federal-provincial co-operation and of integrated action based on commonly perceived priorities. To stress again the central point, all such assessments will take place within a total analytical spectrum and future action will be aimed at ensuring maximum over-all efficiency, effectiveness and co-ordination of total government social security expenditure. It is felt that this method is superior to simply piling more patches on top of existing patches in a social security quilt that is already too short in some places and too threadbare in others.
We ought to look at costs. How much will such programs cost the Canadian people? Without going into too many details, I wish to consider economic costs, social costs and costs to the financial community in general. The economic costs must be considered and I stress the need for an in-depth analysis of this area. When considering economic costs, factors such as the loss of trained manpower must be considered, early retirement provisions may induce certain highly skilled and trained members of our work force to retire from active employment at an age below which less skilled workers might consider retiring.
We must consider, also, the ability of people to pay for early retirement. On the one hand, early retirement will reduce the working life of such people but will increase the cost of pensions, and on the other hand, such early retirement will reduce the ability of the economy to produce the level of real income that is needed to support a program of early retirement. We must also consider under economic costs the drop in income. Even generous pensions will provide less than can be realized by wages. In some cases the pension will not meet a person's needs and that person, after retiring, will be forced to seek social assistance.
We must also consider the social cost to the Canadian people. We must consider the problem of health. Studies show that the status of employment is a determining factor in the health of the elderly who are employed, however, this is not the only consideration to be borne in mind. Retirement from employment may have adverse effects on one's health, even if one's physical condition had remained constant prior to retirement. Also, will earlier retirement result in increased institutional care costs for senior citizens, as well as increased housing costs for senior citizens who cannot find suitable accommodation in
December 3, 1974

the private market, at a price they can afford once their income has been reduced?
Finally, one must consider the social consequences of early retirement or the negative public image of an elderly person. Will persons who retire early be willing to face the prevalent, negative image attached to elderly persons or to those who retire before retirement age?
As well, we must bear in mind the increased costs to be borne by the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan in cases of early retirement. Will early retirement bring about labour-management difficulties, or will such retirement in special areas bring about specific labour shortages? I stress these points as they must be considered. It is the Canadian public who will be asked to support such programs. Increased taxes may be necessary if we are to support people who retire at an earlier age.
In conclusion, I remind hon. members opposite that the aims of their motion are not feasible at this time due to the greater needs of the Canadian people which must be attended to by the Government of Canada in ensuring that all Canadians will benefit. To state without further ado that the age of retirement should be lowered to 60, when many feel that they should not retire even at 65, is to put forward a most uncompromising proposition to the people of Canada. The overriding principle is that we must do what we can for the Canadian people, but we must resist at this time, what is proposed in view of new legislation affecting the Canada Pension Plan and measures proposed in the budget.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECTED TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to take part in this debate on the motion introduced by my colleagues of the Social Credit Party, and I would like to congratulate them for having introduced such a motion in this House. I would also like to urge the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) to consider very carefully that need of those 60 years of age and over.
I would like to confess at once, Mr. Speaker, that I do not intend to take up the time allotted to me to indulge in negative criticism-quite the opposite. I would not want to be one of those who would simply say that the minister did not make any efforts. On the contrary, I know that the minister did make efforts to deal with the difficulties facing those people, proposed solutions and is now discussing with the provinces this guaranteed annual income which I think is an excellent thing.
The government is now considering with the provinces three plans of guaranteed minimum income. This is somewhat of an urgent necessity if we want to make our social security system more simple, more consistent and more effective, and especially if we want to put up a better fight against poverty.
The studies under way on income security and eventually a guaranteed minimum income are a central point in the debates and the needs of today. The present social programs and the old age security pension are currently under consideration for people of 65 years of age.
Following the many arguments that were put to me, and I think the same arguments were raised in other ridings, I
Old Age Pensions
personally conducted a survey in my riding. Out of 6,000 answers, 98 per cent were in favour of old age security at 60, but with the choice left to the individual so that he might either take a deserved retirement or continue to work when in very good health.
I would like to seize this opportunity to seek the minister's support so that the matter will receive particular attention and I invite him to consider the possibility.
I shall certainly be told that the government has already increased the old age security and welfare allowances. True, it has done so; we know perfectly well that it had to do it considering the cost of living. I have no intention whatsoever of repeating that the government has not considered the social security problem, but I believe there is urgency and personally I agree 100 per cent with the Social Credit motion before us today.
As for the comments I get in my riding, I have every reason to believe other members in other ridings are told the same things. How far should the government go in financing such a program? We might discuss the matter later on.
I think we should consider seriously the possibility of allowing people over 60 to take a well deserved rest. I believe that if we fail to consider that question today, when we are perfectly aware of the present situation, we may be facing old age security at 55 within 10 or 15 years. In my opinion, we would make a colossal mistake if we refused to give that matter every necessary consideration. I believe that is nearly seven years, since I represent my riding, I have never hesitated once nor have I missed once the opportunity to recommend that measure, and I think I was right.
We undoubtedly keep hearing of the expense and the possible cost of such a step. However, no one has ever been able to figure out the cost of maintaining 400,000 or 500,000 unemployed people. I believe manpower mobility would provide young men and women with job opportunities when they graduate from universities and often find with disgust that there are no jobs available for them. This would be a positive step for those young people, if we consider that 25 per cent of them are under 25 and claim unemployment insurance benefits.
There are apparently 786,000 people between the ages of 60 and 65. It might be possible to grant old age pensions as of 1975 for a period of five years to 64 year old people. According again to 1971 figures, there were at the time 145,000 people of 64 years of age.
I believe the implementation of such a measure, along with the implementation of the guaranteed annual income as mentioned by the Minister, might be extremely worthwhile. However, this is apparently not for the near future. Nevertheless the government is still thinking of that step which I think is very worthwhile, but if we consider the situation of people 65 years old especially in the light of technical changes in our industry, we know perfectly well that the same machine in any industry is running a lot faster than it was 15, 20 or even 30 years, ago. Therefore, these people who never had to rush during their working hours are quite unable to keep up with this modern technology, and if we really want to humanize the industrial

December 3, 1974
Old Age Pensions
sector, we feel the need to apply this measure, and many of those would certainly be willing to retire at 60.
We must also consider the case of the wife who is not 65 yet. We could at least go even further than the proposal put forward by the government and take into consideration the fact that the wife under 65 who cannot receive a pension puts the couple in a very difficult position, something which is not provided for at the present time.
I would like to urge the minister to reconsider his position as concerns the granting of old age security at 60.
I said that in 1968 we had 175,000 unemployed, and I sincerely believe that we could have eliminated the problems caused by this unemployment rate. Apparently to fight inflation, the unemployment rate was increased starting in 1968, but we find ourselves, and I say this without malice, with 400,000 to 500,000 unemployed and we still have inflation to boot. If we look at the figures for 1971, we see that there were 800,000 people between 60 and 65. Had we granted old age security at 60 over five years, I believe that we would have solved the unemployment problem which worsened from year to year, while allowing those who wanted to do so to take a well-deserved rest.
In my constituency, for instance, there are approximately 3,000 people aged 60 to 65; there are not necessarily 3,000 unemployed. I believe that if we had lowered the retirement age to 64 in 1968, to 63 in 1969, and so on, we would have gone a long way towards solving the unemployment problem, which is extremely expensive.
Once again, I would urge the government or the minister responsible to consider this. We must admit that a government must be very serious and do some serious thinking before implementing a program which would apparently cost more than $1 billion. I believe we should also take into account the advantages of such legislation and the savings that it could bring about by reducing unemployment.
I wonder if, up to a point, it would involve anything more than the reallocation of certain funds, which would give a holiday to those who deserve it and benefit the young people who are still looking for jobs.
Those are the few comments I wanted to make on this motion, Mr. Speaker. But I was also thinking of the morale of the worker, for instance. We are well aware that several workers deplore the fact that social measures apply to some individuals who, without, work, often give the impression to the workers that they are more intelligent than they are.
As far as the worker is concerned, the tax levied on his wages is used once again to enable other people to remain unemployed.
I think that if such a measure were enforced, the worker would be willing and pleased to contribute to such a legislation, because at 60 years of age, he would take it seriously. Today his contributions would allow his parents to take a rest thanks to an adequate pension. I think that he would be pleased to do so. As a result, the worker would have a much greater motivation than he has today because of increased benefits which would be very costly to the government.
(Mr. La Salle.]
We are considering a specific motion which should ensure that such a measure would be to the advantage of the community. Consequently, I will not hesitate in due time, if we have to vote, to support such a motion, because it would give those people a chance to have a well deserved rest, and would also he highly beneficial both to our younger and older citizens and to all those who are looking for jobs. Given the context of a society undergoing tremendous changes, we owe it to ourselves to reconsider the legislation before us.
It is not enough, I think, to consider the possibility of having people retire at the age of 60. It is also our duty to consider the overall social aspect of the measure and the social context in which these people are living.
I think it is advisable and urgent, before undertaking any further studies, to have the basis of the old age security programs changed so that the qualifying age for pension be set between 60 and 65 in harmony with all the social programs which the Minister is now considering, and this in co-operation with the provinces. I think it would be appropriate to have this matter considered in relation with people who have reached age 60.
I also suggest that if we want to do something beneficial and humanitarian for those people, we should also consider whatever relates to this category of people such as transportation, for example. We know that this group of people often ask for certain privileges or certain benefits in connection with transportation, housing or lodging, medical prescriptions, home care and a whole list of services.
I would even go so far as to say that when the government implemented the New Horizons Program they deserved to be congratulated. They showed extraordinary initiative but it still seems that for these people the government is still short of funds. I think it is our responsibility to co-operate in promoting and organizing their leisure time and an interesting life from age 60 though the limit is now set at 65, but could be 60.
I think that a social policy for this category of people should take all those aspects into account and deal with them with all due attention. Adequate allowances are very important for them. It is important to consider the wife who unfortunately is not eligible because of her age. Whether we want it or not, we must absolutely do it. Secondly, all these factors which are part of the life of any individual at that age must be provided for in a general program which will definitely give these people a further lease on life, the benefits they are entitled to and the possibility of doing something by way of recreation.
So with these comments, Mr. Speaker, I am once again very objectively asking the minister to consider these possibilities and pass these measures as soon as possible. We know that in the primary industries there are workers aged 60 who are terribly eager to retire. And I think that such comments are received from all ridings and they are heard very often. I think that introducing this motion in the House was a good thing. As a member of this House I think it is fair to recommend this to the attention of the minister and I would be very happy to support the government if they presented us tomorrow with a similar proposal to fulfill the needs of thousands of individuals.
