speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my calculations amount to four billion dollars. Here, Mr. Minister, are the billions- four billion dollars, that is two thirds of the whole budget of the province of Quebec.
That is very easy. I noticed, for that matter, that the previous speaker, the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), goes hard at it when he says this, very piously, and he is not the only member of the opposition who talked very piously this afternoon-everybody here is particularly religious on that subject today, whereas I contend that it is a public lie to deceive the people into thinking that we can afford this immediately-he says he would with great pleasure vote with the Creditistes on this resolution if it were put, while knowing very well-for he has been in this House long enough-that this resolution does not call for a vote, since it expires automatically under Standing Order 58(11). I find it a little easy for one to advocate something one knows very well one will never be able to put into practice. That amounts to telling the people, who do not have the same reference documents as we do, things that they are not in a position to check for themselves.
Going rapidly over the present situation, we know that old age pension was granted in 1952. At that time there was no guaranteed income supplement, and the pension only consisted in a monthly $40. A more flexible system was implemented in 1967 to alleviate the situation of people who were really in need. The concept of a guaranteed income according to needs was introduced, and both amounts have of course gone up steadily. It may not be as high as we might hope, for we can never ask for too much on behalf of old people. And that very feeling of guilt that we all share in respect of retired people is currently being taken advantage of with all that fuss about the alleged emergency to lower immediatly the retirement age for everyone, and to multiply the amounts to be paid under that program.
I think people's emotions are being manipulated-at least they were considerably manipulated during the electoral campaign-for in our days when the bulk of population concentrates in towns where families do not have sufficient accommodation to keep their old parents, and when provincial governments, in many instances, have
1902

December 3, 1974
Old Age Pensions
unfortunately not provided for the creation of a sufficient number of homes for the aged where required, it is unfortunately too easy to suggest that we have not done enough, and that the government is deliberately disregarding older people.
Let me add that I for one believe that pension age should not be lowered to 60, and that the time is not right. I think it should be received at 55, and this should have been done 30 years ago. I see the problem in a different light. Let me explain: 55-year-old people-and I am concerned with real problems, not with easy and reverent phrases-55-year-old people can easily and could, 20 or 30 years ago, be overly tired, for they generally worked in physically exhausting and often unacceptable social conditions.
Canadians have today the highest life expectancy in the world, namely 76 for women and between 72 and 74 for men. I no longer have the precise figures, but women do not die easily! Although I do not have the detailed statistics, I want to say that the higher our life expectancy, the more a lower pensionable age would be sought, without the least thought of facing the music and considering the problem, the possible consequences of employment interruption that would be forced upon a whole segment of the population.
I must say at this point that for every letter I received during the election campaign asking me to lower the pensionable age to 60, I got one asking me to retain the right to work for people in the same age group. Then the universality principle so dear to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who asserted it no later than a few days or a few weeks ago is then open to question and challenged.
I do not feel that this matter can be so easily solved. As I said, I am interested in real concrete problems and not so much in ideologies easy to convey, because quite emotional, but which are deceiving the man in the street.
We would have to dismiss suddenly and arbitrarily all labour force between 60 and 65 years of age if we wish to maintain universality. This could directly make some people ill due to the disruption of their way of living, because in the Canadian community, the social institutions are not organized to meet the new needs of the group between 60 and 65 years of age who would be more and more active as a result of the increased longevity of the Canadian people.
It is a problem which the Creditists have not yet solved. I repeat that I would have like to see that measure applied 30 years ago, but if it was not, I think that we can sincerely say that the economic possibilities of the federal budget, perhaps also the lack of general sensibility did not allow it, but there was probably no bad faith involved.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I will point out three extremely urgent problems which should be solved when referring to the needs of senior citizens.
The hon. parliamentary secretary mentioned Several of those among which I would like to deal with one in particular. She mentions here social priorities in general, and not only those of people over 60 years old. Among

Canadian social priorities, I would like to deal with that of single parent families in need. I will add to this three concrete problems which, in my opinion, are especially related to the last part of the second half of life. First, the employment problem for all those who lose their job after 50. I am obviously talking about the problem in large cities, which is the one I know best. The unwritten but very real discrimination of employers against any unemployed individual who has to write down on his forms that he is 51, 52, 53 years old and even more, even if he is in perfect health, should be erased from our traditions as quickly as possible.
Second, there is the urgent social problem of older single people, very often women, who had to bring up their brothers and sisters or help their aged parents and who, because of the structure of our society, did not have any special professional or technical training and who, at 50 or 60, do not receive any assistance from other members of the family and find themselves alone after having lost the parents to whom they devoted their life.
Thirdly, I wish to mention the couples who will be covered by the government proposal which we hope will be implemented in January 1975, couples in which one of the spouses is not yet of retirement age, that is couples who must suddenly start living on the pension of a single person after living on a salary and who obviously cannot manage it.
Mr. Speaker, I would have many other things to say about this problem which is very important to Canadians. It is obvious that everyone would like the retirement age lowered, and indeed, not even to 60. Some people who are 30 years old would also like it to be lowered. A great many people would like to see the retirement age lowered as soon as possible. All members of this House certainly want everything possible to be done for senior citizens. This is a basis of common understanding about which there is a consensus.
However, Mr. Speaker, I shall never accept that they tell stories to lead our people to believe that a budget which represents over two third of that of the entire province of Quebec can be found like this, without even saying from where it would come.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECTED TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to support the motion moved today in this House by my very good friend and colleague, the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise), a motion which reads as follows:
This House regrets that the Government neglected to make all those who reached the age of 60, as well as their spouses although such spouses may not have reached pensionable age, eligible for the Old Age Pension.
I want more particularly to thank and congratulate my colleague for having moved such a motion in the House on a number of occasions. I feel that it will mark an era, because it repeats what the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was saying during the last election campaign. It aims at bringing the case of senior citizens before the House, so that they may be allowed to retire at age 60 on an optional basis. I do not agree with the previous speaker that this motion provides for universal retirement at age 60. The purpose of our motion is to lower to 60 the retirement age, but on a voluntary basis, that is for those who
December 3, 1974

want it, in addition to enable the spouse of a retired person to automatically receive the old age security pension.
I consider that this is a major problem which is not easy to deal with but which requires a great deal of tact if one is to discuss it objectively. However, this problem is quite real and is becoming increasingly serious due to the ever rising cost of living. Faced with this situation, the government must take prompt action, and I feel the only position that the hon. members can take is to pursue a common goal without animosity or political partisanship, that is to find solutions as quickly as possible.
I intend, Madam Speaker, during the few minutes at my disposal, to look at what has been done up to now in various places, in order to put this debate in its true perspective. Afterwards, since this motion contains three aspects, I intend to talk first of all about the lowering of the retirement age to 60, then about the automatic eligibility to pension of the spouse and finally I will deal with the voluntary retirement for those who are between 60 and 65 years of age.
If we consider the historical background of this motion, and if we look at what is being done elsewhere, we first realize that opinions on the retirement age vary considerably according to economic requirements and special situations that occur during the life of a nation.
In times of unemployment, as is now the case in Canada, the public opinion requires that retiring age be lowered so that more older people may leave the labour market and give way to younger workers. On the other hand, it must be pointed out that the difficulty which older workers are facing to find a job also contributes to the need for lowering the retirement age. That is what happend in Denmark in 1932, when labour unions asked that retirement age be reduced from 65 to 60. The same reactions have led the British trade unions to advocate a lower retirement age and a higher limit for compulsory school attendance so as to make jobs available for young people and find them more work. It can then be said that it is the needs which guide the decisions of the countries in that connection.
One notices also that this problem is not a new one and that long before us other countries recognized the need to lower the pension age and passed legislation to that effect, an Act was even passed in New Zealand in 1898, to grant a pension to men and women of 60 or over. An amendment passed in 1911 in that same country lowered the pension age to 60 for men and to 55 for women, whenever the claimants had two or more dependent children of 15 or under.
Another amendment passed in 1913 granted superannuation pensions to all persons of 60 or over.
The act passed in Australia in 1908 granted superannuation pensions to men and women of 65 or over. That minimum age was lowered to 60 in 1910 and as far as I know, Australia did not go bankrupt as a result. The same amendment also provided that permanently handicapped men could retire at 60.
In Canada for instance, we had to wait until 1927 for a $20 monthly pension in the case of people of 70 or over.
Old Age Pensions
All that, madam Speaker, goes to show that the problem exists in all countries, at least in the industrialized ones, and that as far as Canada is concerned, it took perhaps a little more time to get worse on account of the favourable economic context of the twenties. But I believe that state of the economy which was considered favourable in 1920 has changed now and that time has come for us to consider lowering the pension age to 60, a year at a time if necessary.
I come now to the main point of this motion, namely the lowering, progressive or not, from 65 to 60, of the age of eligibility to the old age security pension. There exist, with regard to that age level, special and often trying problems that could be solved or at least reduced with the lowering of the pension age.
Madam Speaker, there are people between 60 and 65 who do not earn enough and who have to depend on parents or on welfare and must beg for this or that in order to provide for their essential needs.
There are also the sick people who in spite of their poor health do their utmost to go to work until they reach the pension age, namely the age of 65. I represent a riding where several big factories or industries, mines or paper-mills are located. I often receive comments from those workers, the great majority of which would like to have the alternative to retire at 60. Mrs. Speaker, I want that point to be understood clearly! They write that they would like to have that alternative.
Furthermore, in asbestos mills such as those in Asbestos and Thetford and in papermills such as those in Brompton and Windsor in my riding, additional problems have appeared those last few years, namely the outbreak of diseases called industrial diseases.
There is also the fact that faced with economic difficulties, industries and factories demand an ever increasing output from their employees, whatever be their age; this affects the elder in a particular way and often contributes directly to shorten their lives.
Moreover, the pension at 60 would enable several younger healthy people in the bloom of youth to replace the elder willing to retire.
Furthermore, such a measure would remove the difficulties for those between 60 and 65 who are laid off for lack of capacity and do not manage to get back on the labour market.
Madam Speaker, when the Western industrial giants like Chrysler Canada Ltd., Ford Motor Company of Canada Limited and the like lay off thousands of workers such as is presently the case due to the economic crisis, the same happens with smaller enterprises. That means more and more massive lay-offs and those less able to find a new job are still the oldest workers. Hence the urgent need for adequate solutions like the one we are proposing. There are several points in favour of lowering the age of retirement, but I referred to the most important ones.
Now I should like to talk a little about the second principle in the motion before us, namely to give automatically the pension to the wife of a pensioner.
In the present circumstances, it seems to me more and more necessary that the wife of a pensioner also receive a
28543-52%

December 3, 1974
Old Age Pensions
pension simultaneously. My constituents strongly advocated this approach and the problems submitted to us are often very distressing. For example, we have the case of the husband who retires at 65, but who is the only one to get a pension because his wife is younger than he is; often, the wife will work if she can still do so; she will work hard sometimes. She will clean floors or do similar tasks, or she will ask her member of the legislative assembly to write to the welfare people to get her a pittance from the provincial government.
I think that in 1974, the situation has lasted long enough and that we should give a pension to the wife as soon as the husband gets his.
Turning to another aspect, Madam Speaker, we propose that those between 60 and 65 not be forced into retirement but rather that they may do so if they consider it suitable.
Major objections were in fact raised, and often rightly so, about the fact that compulsory retirement would sometimes create serious problems. That is not the case for the sick, the handicapped, the non-retrainable, or those for whom it is impossible to go back to work. On the other hand, such a compulsory measure could be prejudicial to those who have obligations up until the age of retirement or even are in good health and want to continue working until 65.
The best answer to all those problems is what we are now proposing, that the pension at age 60 be optional and up to the individual. Several difficulties would thus be avoided, and the freedom of the individual would be upheld.
Madam Speaker, I am under the impression that the government should now be in a position to accept our motion, at least follow it up very soon with very specific measures since several members on the government side including the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), as well as the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stressed the soundness of such measures as well as their principles in that respect.
To illustrate that the attitude of this government is in line with our motion, I would simply like to refer to statements made during the last election campaign in the month of July 1974. There was talk about the subject-matter of our motion today in the context of the "integrated system of social security" as laid before the people of Canada by the Liberal party in power during the last general election. For example, in the newspaper Le Droit of June 21, 1974, quoting from an article by Fay Lariviere:
Sherbrooke-The Prime Minister restated Thursday his intention of providing Canada with a revised and integrated social security system in cooperation with the provinces in line with the guidelines set out in the working paper of April 1973 tabled in the Commons by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, Mr. Marc Lalonde.
The first measure implemented will be to extend the benefits, subject to a means test, to the wife of an old age security pensioner if she is between 60 and 65.
However small, it would be at least be a first step, a gesture indicating an intention to improve the situation in this area. All the more as since then, the cost of living has kept increasing. The situation has become even more difficult for people of 60.
Recently, in his budget speech, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) announced some tax cuts for lower income

groups, thus showing his willingness to deal with the difficulties caused by our economic situation. It was all very well, but I feel it is time for us to do something about pensionable age.
Madam Speaker, every political party saw fit to raise the matter during the election campaign. The time has now come for the members to act. For all these reasons, I believe that now more than ever it is time to do something positive or at least to give the Canadian people an inkling about it.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have listened religiously to the previous speakers during this debate on the motion of the Social Credit Party. I agree entirely with the hon. member for Saint-Michel (Miss Begin), and I think it would be rather expensive to implement such a program.
But before I expound my philosophy on this subject, I would point out to the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) that, in my opinion, the Progressive Conservative Party has a short memory. I must explain because the hon.
December 3, 1974

member for Joliette stated at great length during the election campaign what he has just said.
But I have here an official document on the elections of the last few years. I notice that under the Progressive Conservative government from 1957 to 1963 the pension plan was only increased by $10 in seven years, that is less than $1.50 a year. We can then appreciate the record of the Progressive Conservative party as regards the old age security pension.
As soon as the liberals were elected in 1963, the increase was by $10, and a comparison between both records will show that under the liberals, the pension was increased from $75 in 1963 to an amount of $117.02, in October 1974, with an escalation clause, which added to the guaranteed income supplement comes to $199.10 for single people and $189.91 for a married couple.

speechtext:
And the Minister just tells me that this amount will be increased to $204 in January.
Madam Speaker, such was the performance of the Progressive Conservative Party when it was in power regarding that policy, compared with the Liberal government's performance. I would raise the following question: it now seems much easier for the Conservatives to take a stand on social measures than on the oil problem. There is no unanimity in that area, because the problem seems complicated, but on social measures, they are asking for more and more and once again, we see nothing wrong with that.
Madam Speaker, when I was asked to speak today I sought inspiration in a document I have here and entitled "Je ne demande que de servir". We find in it the words of a man of extraordinary energy and courage. Here are the words of His Excellency Governor General Georges Vanier, and I quote:
Old age does not come from the number of years lived. I firmly believe we get old only when we relinquish our ideal. Indeed, the symptoms of old age are fear and discouragement, while youth is characterized by an attitude of health and confidence, especially toward young ones.
Nowadays, attraction is toward material things. We have a tendency to stress standard of living rather than the aim of life.
In passing judgment on a social policy, it is not enough to blame the government for not bringing pensionable age down to 60. We all strive for social betterment; but improvements in this area, or in the field of economic development, are not brought about by random attempts or by momentaneous pressures. They have to be planned, with the cooperation of all the people and every social agency, both at the preparation and implementation stage. According to Statistics Canada, the 65-year old and above will number 2.5 million in 1985, a 47 per cent increase over the last census. Extrapolation indicates for the year 2000 an extra 700,000, 88 per cent more than in the 1971 census. All this points to a well planned program. Social improvement is an essential factor in economic development, to the extent it helps improve human resources.
Old Age Pensions
Madam Speaker, I would like to deal in the next few minutes with another aspect of today's debate.
I do not pretend to be an expert on old age. I would like nonetheless to give my humble views, even if they are not shared by members opposite. The latter I would refer to as "today's spendthrifts". They propose the most simplistic, the most materialistic of solutions, namely reducing pensionable age to 60 without any other consideration.
Of course, I cannot take the time to elaborate on all the social measures proposed by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), or to explain the general aims of the social programs that are being reviewed with the provinces, from the guaranteed income to the community employment policy, keeping in mind those who have special needs.
Having said this, I shall now restrict myself to the 1972 program which shows the importance given by the government to the plight of the older citizen in our society. This program called "New Horizons" clearly shows the willingness of this same government to explore new avenues and implement novel formulas when they appear likely to meet adequately the needs of those who have reached the third age.
What is the thrust of this program?
First of all, this program gives older people the opportunity to contribute to their own welfare as well as that of the community. Secondly, the program is designed to help the government to set up effective means of communication and liaison with the pensioners and the aged, in order to make them aware of their needs and to provide for the passage of the required measures. And thirdly, the program seeks to bring about a general awareness through which an attempt will be made to grasp the meaning of the word "aging" in the context of our modern life.
The hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) stated a while ago that the 60-year old would like to retire as soon as possible. I think that it is less and less true on the contrary. Still again, I agree with the member for Saint-Michel (Miss Begin). If we consider that there is less physical effort than 25 years ago, that the number of working days has decreased as well as the number of working hours, I think that the statement of the hon. member for Joliette to the effect that the people would like to retire at 60 years of age is not true. He is playing politics at the expense of those people.
I would like, Madam Speaker, to refer to my father as an example. When he learned that he was pensioned at 65 years of age, he could not accept it. Unfortunately he died a few months later, because he could not get used to the idea that he was retired. He felt that he still had some possibilities and a potential to work for the community. He did not want to be discarded.
The New Horizons Program was designed as an innovation program. This was a deliberate effort in order to try to establish the most flexible program possible whereby the government would be in a position to offer to groups of retired people the financial assistance necessary to implement projects of their choice and thus give free rein to their talent, their abilities, their ingeniousness and the full richness of their experience.

December 3, 1974
Old Age Pensions
Society has often tended to adopt a paternalistic attitude with the programs intended for the aged. Society was inclined to dictate rather than suggest, to act without bothering to consult beforehand the very people on behalf of whom it was acting. That is what we have tried to avoid with the New Horizons Program which is essentially based on self-determination. In the light of our brief experience, we are already in a position to recognize all the resources of invention, energy and collective goodwill shown by the aged. As they are able to identify their own needs, develop projects which interest them and plan them in conjunction with their needs and as they have been faced with many obstacles and have learned to foresee them, they know now how to assess the kind of support they will have to ask for; briefly, senior and retired citizens are now in a position to call upon all their possibilities and their experience which otherwise could not be fully exploited. But there is more: there is the spirit of enthusiasm they generate the incredible vitality which emanates from their projects; both have repercussions on the whole of society and contribute, in a way, to erase the obsolete concepts about senior citizens and to replace them by an image more akin to reality.
Madam Speaker, I have here the list of the projects that were accepted since the beginning of this federal program. The number of projects by province is extraordinary and we can see how the projects submitted fill almost unbelievable needs. They are part of a most remarkable spirit of innovation and enthusiasm. To date, since the beginning of this program, 2,960 projects have been approved for a total of $21,393,143.
How many retired people benefit from or participate in the implementation of these projects? There are 635,128 retired people who are concerned with various New Horizons projects.
Since I cannot table the paper, if I may, Madam Speaker, I will indicate the number of projects by province, simply to demonstrate how that program was overwhelmingly popular throughout Canada.
In Newfoundland, 47 projects were approved, amounting to $294,173. In Prince Edward Island, 35 projects were approved, totalling $132,692. In Nova Scotia, 66 projects were approved for an amount of $732,905. In New Brunswick, 111 projects were approved for an amount of $661,254. In Quebec, 752 projects were approved, totalling $4,072,592. In Ontario, 976 projects were approved and the minister is telling me that they amounted to $5,469,653. The minister certainly is aware of the amounts of money granted by his department and he would like to see the figures quoted accurately by all members.
In Manitoba, 201 projects were approved to an amount of $932,800; in Saskatchewan, 232 projects totalling $931,342; in Alberta, 189 projects for $1,124,975; in British Columbia, 345 projects for $1,920,231. For the Northwest Territories, four projects were approved for a total of $24,921 and two projects in the Yukon, amounting to $9,037. As I mentioned earlier, the total amount is $21,393,143.
Madam Speaker, I believe that the sampling carried out throughout Canada for these projects proves how much

our senior citizens and our pensioners want to continue working for the development of Canada.
In conclusion, I congratulate the hon. Minister and I thank him on behalf of all those people who, from October 1975, will receive a pension, as a temporary measure, which will provide assistance for a couple when one spouse retires at 65 and two people must live on a single pension. This agreement was discussed at length in the Liberal caucus and I was very glad when the minister confirmed it. It is not realistic to think that we shall solve all our social security problems by paying millions of dollars to all people between 60 and 65 who may not need it. It would be better to implement a program which guarantees the income with no age restriction for those who are unemployed, handicapped or do not have a sufficient salary.
Madam Speaker, I would like to close with this sentence of Felix Leclerc: The best way to make a man die is to stop him from working. I therefore prefer to keep in mind the positive aspect of our program rather than say that we shall provide money regardless of need.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECT TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity which enables me to take part in this afternoon's debate. Having listened to members' contributions, I detect a reasonable degree of unanimity in our approach to the problem we are considering.
The previous speaker, the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Roy), spoke of the bad old days and seemed to identify them exclusively with one party. I do not think he deliberately meant to leave the wrong impression this afternoon. If he casts his mind back to 1956, I think he will remember the attitude shown by the then Liberal government to old age pensioners. That attitude resulted in a popular slogan being adopted in the election of 1957. All hon. members will recall what happened in the 1957 election. We saw the day of deliverance when, at long last, there was a change of government. Because of the parsimonious attitude of the outgoing Liberal government and of the then minister of finance to the funding of pensions for senior citizens of Canada, members of that government became known across the country as "the six buck boys."
This afternoon we shall not talk about the bad old days, as it is clear that in the last 15 years or so, beginning with the change of government in 1957, we have seen a new, more positive and constructive approach to the problem of meeting the social needs of the people of Canada.
As I already indicated, I do not think there is much disagreement on the broad fundamentals in achieving the objective that we all want to attain, that is, an adequate level of income, not only for our elderly but for all groups who find themselves in a position where they are not able to earn sufficient income for a reasonable standard of living. Along with the elderly that could include those who have disabilities such as the blind, the severely disabled, and those who are handicapped mentally or in any other respect.
December 3, 1974

I congratulate the Social Credit group for having made this debate possible. While I might not agree specifically with their solution to the problem, I am sure the debate that has been precipitated as a result of their motion is going to add a lot of grist to the mill which is now grinding as a result of the presentation of the orange paper by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde).
I shall deal with some aspects of the orange paper, but before I do I should put on the record the fact that the members of the official opposition have been in the vanguard of exploring new ways and means of dealing with the problem of income maintenance for those who are in a needy position. For example, as far back as 1972 the Conservative party came forward with specific recommendations. I shall deal with them briefly.
First, we recommended the establishment of a national income floor for individuals and families who have no earned income because of physical disability or other valid reasons. A second major point was to ensure that an individual or family capable of earning an income below the poverty line is entitled to retain a specific amount of this earned income without any reduction in the amount of public income supplement received. This has been described as the incentives income policy. The third point was to ensure that beyond this first specified amount an individual or family would be entitled to earn an additional amount of money which would be more than that by which the public income supplement would be reduced. That, I repeat, is the policy statement that emanated from members of the official opposition as far back as 1972.
As I read the orange paper recommendations put forward by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, I can only conclude that he must have been looking over the shoulders of the policy formulators of the official opposition. I congratulate him on his wisdom in this regard.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECT TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext:
The principles that have been laid down in the current discussion that is going on with regard to social security parallel very closely those outlined by members of the Conservative party, and I shall quote them.
In the first place, the social security plan shall ensure to persons unable to work, the elderly, the blind, and the disabled, an annual guaranteed income that is fair and compassionate.
I will read the second principle that has been laid down by the minister in his initial statement on the orange paper, because it is germane to our discussion today:
The second principle, the social security system, applicable to persons able to work include work incentives and emphasize the need for reinstatement of social welfare recipients into the labour force.
Those two principles, I submit, are an almost direct paraphrase of the principles laid down in the Conservative party manifesto. Again I congratulate the minister. Of course he at one time had very close identification with members of the official opposition. I am sure that sort of association has had a strong determining tendency on the attitudes of the minister, even though he has fallen amongst bad companions in recent years.
Old Age Pensions
Obviously there has to be action along the lines proposed by the motion because the government itself has now introduced a plan whereby its employees can retire at age 60. In parallel plans several provinces, including my own province of Manitoba, have now made similar retirement without loss of pension benefits available to their numerous employees at age 60.
We are all aware that more and more of the labour force are involved in government operations. One of the issues that emerged in the recent election campaign in my constituency-and we do not have a great number of civil servants at either the provincial or the federal level in the city of Brandon-was the question of when would the government bring its old age security program and Canada Pension Plan into line with its age 60 retirement plan? This is an indication that if we are going to rationalize our social security program we have to deal with inequities sooner or later. In light of the hodge-podge which is now an essential part of our social security system, I would say the sooner the better.
In his peregrinations during the election campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made this one of the major points in his promises, of which there were many. He wants to have the following integrated into the government's social security program for pensioners: the extension of the OAS/GIS on an income tested basis to spouses aged 60 to 64 of the present recipients of the OAS/GIS.
This was to be merely an interim step until such time as the comprehensive review that has been precipitated by the presentation of the orange paper has been completed. The official opposition presented a similar proposition, namely, that there be some consideration for the spouses of husbands or wives, as the case may be, who had reached the age of 65.
In the remaining few moments of the time allotted to me I wish to go into the broader concept of the need for providing income stability to groups other than the elderly. The elderly are in a special category by reason of age. However, there are those who are prematurely handicapped, as I have already indicated, by reason of blindness, physical disability, and handicaps of various other kinds. The strange and even tragic anomaly is that there is no special income allowance for people with handicaps of this kind. Since 1924 the blind people have been asking for a blindness allowance that would be paid regardless of the financial circumstances of the individual or the family concerned. They make this request on the simple basis that blindness is a severe handicap for which there is need for general community support.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) went back to 1927 in his presentation this afternoon. He referred to the great struggle for an adequate income security plan for the elderly. The blind of Canada and their associations have been campaigning for the same consideration for this group of disabled persons since 1924. The physically handicapped are in the same category. Perhaps I can deal with the two together to show how inadequate or even ridiculous the situation can be when governments, either federal or provincial, fail to consider the special needs of the handicapped.

December 3, 1974
Old Age Pensions
In the case of the blind, if two blind persons marry and there is a certain amount of income the wife loses her disability allowance. It is not a generous sum in any case-about $75 a month. Recently I received a letter from two severely handicapped persons, both disabled by cerebral palsy, who married. Before their marriage the wife had been in receipt of a disability allowance of some $75. I have met these two individuals in person. The husband is less severely handicapped than the wife; she is in a wheelchair and is not really able to take care of herself at all.
The enterprising husband in this happy matrimonial situation has employment as a counsellor at the Chedoke Institute in Hamilton and now, because he has a certain income and because he has married a fellow sufferer from cerebral palsy his spouse immediately loses her social benefits. This is an urgent situation which must be dealt with, and I trust it will be attended to by the government when it brings down its more comprehensive recommendations arising from the current review of the orange paper.
Unfortunately, in recent years government involvement in these areas has been going backward rather than forward. After the war, led by the Department of Veterans Affairs, there was a great upsurge in interest in the needs of the disabled. More recently, even though our horizons have extended and we understand better the needs of the disabled with regard to education, vocational training, transportation, accommodation and so forth, there seems to have been fewer effective attempts to provide solutions.
In some parts of Canada, it is true, a beginning has been made, but we have yet to follow the example of some countries where, for instance, one finds a whole range of programs which make it possible for the severely disabled to lead a more or less normal existence notwithstanding their handicaps. Up to the present Canada's approach has left much to be desired.
I know the minister agrees with me because the orange paper suggests he is disillusioned about what has been going on in the past; emphasis has been placed upon trying to put new wine into old bottles, if I may use that figure of * speech-trying to express old policies in new forms and to carry on with the outdated welfare state concept where the outlook of the government is paternalistic.
The new approach is aimed at making it possible for the handicapped to meet their own needs with the help of volunteer groups. This is borne out by the fact that the administrator of research, planning and evolution for the Department of National Health and Welfare, Mr. John Osborne, back in 1973 during a discussion in Watrous, Saskatchewan, concerning the orange paper, asked the voluntary groups working in the area of assistance to the disabled-there are 26 such groups across Canada-to let the government know where it is on the track and where it may have been derailed. I believe the minister will agree that the Canadian approach to these matters has often been off the track-that it has consistently veered off course in recent years.
The parliamentary secretary mentioned cost as being one of the deterrents to moving quickly in this field. She added that there were other demands on public funds. That is true. One of the exorbitant demands on the welfare dollar has come through the Unemployment' Insurance 
Commission. In meeting unemployment insurance demands, overpayments of $2 billion have been made in recent years. There is no need, in a resource rich country like ours, to be faced with these huge demands on the treasury for unemployment. The great mistake is that we have tried to use the Unemployment Insurance Commission as a back door approach to the problems I have briefly outlined this afternoon.
Some of the present ad hoc programs which are geared to nothing specific have also constituted a major drain on the national treasury. I would strongly urge the minister to deal with the specific matters we have been discussing this afternoon. It will not bankrupt Canada. The way the government is spending, with an increase in the budget to $26 billion, it is evident that fiscal policy in Canada must have great flexibility. I urge the government to consider priorities and not expedience.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECT TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I expect all members of the House will readily agree that people who have worked and contributed to their community for some decades should be able to retire, (a) at an age when they are flexible enough to adapt to and enjoy their new lifestyle, and (b) with enough money to provide a decent standard of living. It will be very much harder to find agreement (a) on what is an appropriate retirement age, and (b) how much of a person's financial security in retirement should reasonably be provided by the state, how much by former employers and how much by the individual's own savings.
The motion before the House refers to state pensions being made available at age 60. The age of eligibility set for state pensions has a way of influencing the complusory retirement age. In fact it tends to become the compulsory retirement age. This certainly happened when the pension age was reduced from 70 to 65. The compulsory retirement of an unwilling employee, who is unprepared for retirement either economically or psychologically, can be a painful and unhappy business.
People who are now 60 generally entered the labour force during the depression years and often found it difficult to survive, far less think of saving for their old age, for the first 15 years of their employment. For some there was also war service, followed by resettlement problems afterwards, which further delayed the process of acquiring equity in a pension plan, even where a pension plan was available; and it must be remembered that 40 per cent of the work force is not covered by private group pension arrangements.
While the prevailing rates of old age security and guaranteed income supplement are higher than most provincial social assistance rates for single people and couples, they represent quite a drop in salary for the average Canadian worker. In the riding I represent, where many people do hard manual work, I find considerable interest on the part

December 3, 1974
of middle aged people in relocating to work which is less physically demanding, but very high resistance to the idea of final retirement.
This seems to be a fairly general trend. There is an early retirement option in the public service which provides quite generous superannuation benefits, yet less than 15 per cent of those eligible take up this option. In the blue collar area, the pioneering early retirement plan of the United Auto Workers is very well known, yet the latest take-up figures are less than 20 per cent of those eligible in Canadian plants, and only about 3 per cent of those eligible in the Detroit area, which includes some Canadian workers.
More people seem to be fighting decisions which would retire them early. There was a recent court case concerning the Canadian public service, and there are a number of cases, including many against private companies in the United States, where early retirement is more common. Even very good supplementary private pension rates for early retirees-around $625 a month after 30 years service with the UAW; 60 per cent or more of average earnings in the last five years under superannuation-do not attract large numbers of potential pensioners. So one has perhaps to look past the purely financial reasons at the drop in status which must be adjusted to by the retiring worker.
Desirable or not, our society is strongly work oriented. Individual evaluation, by oneself or by others, often flows from a person's job. In older age brackets this equation of work with social value is particularly strong. Early retirement, especially when involuntary, can drastically harm a retiree's self-image, pride and self-esteem.
Looking at it from another angle, will persons who retire early be willing to face the prevalent attitudes toward elder persons at a much earlier age? We are so concerned with meeting the needs of the aged today that we have given little thought to the future effects of policies on future generations of the aged. As we produce a healthier, better educated and more financially secure older generation, the trend toward earlier retirement may prove to be quite inappropriate.
The success of a retirement depends quite a bit on the amount of preparation for it, such as the development of outside interests and hobbies which can replace the work focus. It is a fallacy to think that just relaxing is something that will satisfy people who have been active all their lives. To be successful these hobbies and interests cannot simply be minor items but must be able to develop into full absorptions.
Pre-retirement training, even at age 65, is a very undeveloped field at the present time. Are we ready to meet the requirements of a whole new retired population? Leisure skills are becoming more and more expensive to acquire and practice. People who are not affluent probably have the least involvement in the hobbies and interests they need to enjoy themselves in the suddenly increased free time they will have.
There is also the whole question of social inter-action. The work place provides a daily set of human contacts, friendships and so on. Retirement removes this meeting place and can bring great loneliness. Low income earners
Old Age Pensions
are least likely to have a set of contacts of which they can make use when retired. Both their physical and social mobility is likely to be limited, and to grow more so as the period of retirement lengthens.
Loss of income, loss of status, loss of friends and the sense of "just hanging around" can be very destructive in respect of a person's self-esteem. Removing something that has been the focus of life for 40 years and replacing it with a void can be harmful. And dropping into retirement status people who are five years younger, more vigorous and more energetic may accentuate this sense of ennui, alienation and uselessness.
A lower pensionable age may be considerably less than a boon to older workers. It may indeed prove harmful to a number of them. People aged 60 who are not employed or are not employable because of illness or disability or, in the case of widows, because of lack of marketable skills, certainly need to have access to financial assistance. However, I do not think that should necessarily be through an early old age pension. Measures now in place include disability and survivors' benefits from the Canada and Quebec pension plans, workmen's compensation and provincial social assistance. I hope that the current social service review will result in a simplified income supplementation which is easier and less expensive to administer, and which is easier for people receiving it to understand and apply for, Mr. Speaker.
An aspect of aging which receives insufficient attention at present is that people are not only living longer, they are staying healthy, active and productive longer. Some people who take advantage of early retirement schemes use their pension to train for and undertake a second career. I do not think state pensions should be used for this purpose but I should like to see a greater interest on the part of industry in encouraging retraining of older workers. I also hope we may find a way to use some of the community employment programs to help older people retrain and relocate.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECT TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to associate myself with the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in congratulating the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise), of the Social Credit party, for introducing this motion in the House today. May I also say I have no difficulty in supporting in principle or spirit any measure to assist our senior citizens with respect to their importance to our community and to our society.
I am one individual in this House who has had perhaps a unique experience with senior citizens. During my years of practice, particularly in my specialty, I have been fortunate to have been in daily contact with senior citizens in my community and in the surrounding area. I can assure you, Sir, I have developed and retain the deepest respect and admiration for this important segment of society.
Members of this House, and indeed all citizens who have not worked with senior citizens or who have not experienced a close personal contact with them, in my view have missed and are missing a rich and rewarding experience. Their philosophy of living is life itself. Their sense of independence, their humour, their faith, and

December 3, 1974
Old Age Pensions
above all their devotion and loyalty to traditions and friends, could well be emulated by many in our present society. I have been privileged to share these experiences with many senior citizens, and have witnessed the important role they have played and continue to play in our society.
During the' debate this afternoon the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Campbell) referred to the necessity of having a comprehensive social program over and above an adequate income support program. In effect the parliamentary secretary indicated the necessity of understanding the total needs of our senior citizens. I support that thesis. I also wish to underscore the necessity of looking at the whole person, the total person, the complete individual.
Perhaps I could best exemplify this by giving one of several examples I have had over the years. I recall that about seven years ago I had occasion to look after an elderly patient who had a heart problem. She had been removed from her own home to live with her family at a distant place. I can assure you that her surroundings were excellent and that the concern and care by her family were unexcelled. Yet despite this the patient continued to deteriorate.
In looking at the total patient I thought it was important to note that what had been overlooked was her sense of independence. The cure, of course, was to return her to her own home where she could live by herself in an environment with familiar people, family and friends she had known over the years. Now, at a young age in her late 80's, she continues to enjoy her surroundings. I think all of us at that time learned a great lesson about independence and the importance of looking at the total patient, the total senior citizen.
During the 1st of March, 1973, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) spoke on old age security. He stated:
... when coupled with the cumulative benefit increases that have been provided, it will be readily seen, Mr. Speaker, that this government has effectively banished poverty for persons over 65 years of age in the course of the last two years.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECT TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see the minister has returned and is listening. I shall certainly take heed of his comments and recheck the record.
I should like to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the minister that my correspondence would not suggest that no senior citizens in our society feel that they have been complimented by the proposals presented by the government. Let me give you one illustration in a letter which I received this past week, part of which reads as follows:

I was wondering if Mr. Turner's budget is final and all the election promises to wives of pensioners have gone down the drain.
Gordon isn't able to do much, and I am trying to keep on selling Watkins to try to get enough to keep going. You know my health, nerves, diabetes, arthritis. It is far from easy to get out in the cold and try to sell to get the necessities that Gordon's pension will not stretch over. It is impossible to keep a home, pay insurances and buy food on one pension for two people. Where are all the promises that we would get my pension in January. I have no choice but try to carry on in the cold until Gordon can (hopefully) help me again.
I just wondered if you could try to stress this fact to a few people like our Prime Minister and Mr. Turner.
I respectfully submit that letter to the minister. As the letter suggests-and this was indicated by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) this afternoon-the recent budget of November 8 offers very little hope and no help to the majority of our senior citizens, and in particular to that great number who are on low and fixed incomes.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) by his own admission, when he presented the budget, gave a very pessimistic economic report for 1975 indicating that inflation would continue. Indeed, it has been estimated that it will continue in double figures during the year 1975. It seems to me that if the government were truly concerned about this important segment of our population, then surely the obvious answer would have been to introduce measures that are anti-inflationary. I recognize that the minister's explanation will be to index old age security and the guaranteed income supplement, but at the same time we must recognize that the problem for this group of citizens is compounded since the basic expenses for old age pensioners for food and housing in particular tend to rise at a much higher rate than the average consumer price index.
I am also concerned when I review the estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1975, and more recently the supplementary estimates, which reveal substantial increases in operating costs. And when I recall the deficit in the unemployment insurance fund of approximately $1 billion I cannot help but question the government's lack of response to social needs in establishing priorities, in particular with respect to our senior citizens.
This afternoon the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said that the motion before us was broad enough to include any aspect of the social security program. I simply want to make reference to two points, and perhaps the minister will comment on them later if he enters the debate. A major problem which frequently works to the disadvantage of our senior citizens is the complexity, the frequent duplication and the fragmentary approach of the social security system. I would like to take one case in point, and that is the guaranteed income supplement.
There are thousands of pensioners who are short of money because of the present system and the inability of the government to introduce alternative proposals which would guarantee the rights of these needy pensioners. This problem is compounded, certainly in my province, by the fact that to qualify for additional money or benefits, such as the 1974 elderly pensioners' tax assistance program for homeowners in Ontario, or for the recent Gains program and for drug assistance the pensioner must be on the guaranteed income supplement.
December 3, 1974

What are some of the questions that they ask? I think I can summarize these from all the correspondence I have. The questions are: Who should apply? What is yearly income? What are qualifying incomes? What yearly income qualifies a single pensioner? What yearly income qualifies a married couple where both are pensioners? What yearly income qualifies a married couple where only one is a pensioner? I suggest seriously to you, Mr. Speaker, that the majority of senior citizens do not have the information available or the answers to the questions, and I think that they are penalized because of it.
I find it inexcusable that many pensioners who are eligible for the guaranteed income supplement have not applied because of the complexity of the system. Surely the government and the Minister of National Health and Welfare in particular, could find and provide alternative proposals to correct the situation and to help these needy pensioners. Perhaps the minister will comment on this problem before the termination of this debate.
The second point I want to make is with reference to the letter that I quoted earlier in which reference was made to the hardships experienced by senior citizens when both husband and wife must try to survive on a single pension. As has been pointed out by others during this debate, surely this matter deserves thoughtful consideration by the government.
As I indicated at the outset, I was impressed with the parliamentary secretary's observation that it is necessary to look at the total social program affecting our senior citizens. During her speech this afternoon she made reference to medical care. It is important for our elderly citizens, as part of a comprehensive program, to look after these individuals. While I support the principles that were enunciated by the parliamentary secretary, I cannot let the government's record go unchallenged, and indeed that record does not reveal the existence of a program dealing with the specific health problems of the aged.
Let me take a moment or two to try to place the problem in its proper perspective. This group of citizens aged 65 and over represents approximately 8 per cent of our total population, or about 1.7 million Canadians. Projections of populations indicate that by the mid 1980's this group will represent approximately 9 per cent of the total population, or about 2.3 million people.
During 1969, 39.9 million days were used by Canadians in hospital treatment in all age groups, and of this total, 13.3 million days of hospital care were used by the 65 and over age group alone. In effect, 33 per cent of hospital days were used by only 8 per cent of the population. Significantly, in this older age group accidents and muscolo-ske-letal disorders are vastly more important in women, while men suffer predominantly from cancer, respiratory and genito-urinary tract disorders.
The average length of stay in hospital for all ages is 12.6 days for men and 11.4 for women. By the age of 75 and over, the length of stay increased to 27.2 for men and 35.2 for women. Clearly, these chronic and disabling diseases are of major significance. Once again it must be stated that our priorities for research, prevention, treatment and rehabilitation are obvious to all those who look at the statistics. However, these disturbing facts do not represent the total picture of disability and despair that is frequent-
Old Age Pensions
ly suffered by our senior citizens. Far too often our aging population is isolated, alone and needlessly rejected in the every day life of modern society. Too often capable expertise is retired only to be forgotten or otherwise ignored. I believe this attitude must, and can be changed.
All of us in this House recognize the importance of young energetic workers, but it is essential that senior citizens continue to be productive to society and to themselves. There is no doubt that the mental health of our senior citizens can be enhanced through continuing productive participation. There are many sectors of our everyday economy which continue to require the parttime assistance, consultation and advice which are available from senior citizens.
I would suggest that the Minister of National Health and Welfare, perhaps in conjunction with the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras), should look carefully at the possibility of developing an inventory of senior citizens across Canada who would be readily available to provide their services when required.
We must also realize that the aging process is frequently related to many simple discomforts of life that can be resolved with prompt intervention and a little expense. For example, nutritional disorders can be linked to buying power or to the lack of properly fitting dentures. The lack of glasses and hearing aids is a major disadvantage. I believe that these problems can be resolved easily through co-ordinated action by the provincial and federal governments, and I hope that the minister will initiate discussions with the provinces to accomplish this.
Again, chronic disorders contribute a great deal to the personal discomfort of far too many aging Canadians. Our preoccupation has been with the provision of treatment facilities, often at the sacrifice or lack of provision of rehabilitation facilities, particularly as they affect these older aged groups. I would encourage the minister to concentrate on this problem and take it up with his provincial counterparts as a priority item in future federal-provincial conferences.
Many additional hardships are experienced by our senior citizens, Mr. Speaker, such as drug costs, high cost of housing, and the inaccessibility of New Horizons programs particularly in rural communities. I would simply conclude by restating that any social program for senior citizens must include adequate income support and a complete understanding of and sympathetic response to the entire individual.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECT TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, without ado, I want to say I am extremely pleased to make my most sincere contribution on that important question of old age security and the Canada Pension Plan.
To repeat what has been said earlier by some of my colleagues, this government did promise to the Canadian people that effective October 1975, allowances would be paid to spouses of old age security beneficiaries aged between 60 and 65 and provision would be made to also remove some of the requirements concerning Canadians

December 3, 1974
Old Age Pensions
who have lived outside of Canada for a limited period of time.
The motion reads as follows:
This House regrets that the Government neglected to make all those who reached the age of 60. as well as their spouses although such spouses may not have reached pensionable age, eligible for the old age pension.
For many years, the Creditistes have been advocating that pensions provided under the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan should be paid to any individual having reached age 60 and increased to $200 a month for single persons as well as married men and to $150 a month for the spouse whatever may be her age.
Mr. Speaker, as time passes, we realize that the cost of living steadily continues to increase, that people on low income such as older people and others, that the retired do not have adequate incomes to live decently, and sometimes they must even do without the basic necessities and even the indispensable. Furthermore, since there are a lot of married women who have not yet reached the age of 60 and have no source of income they often find themselves in awkward situations.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that each time I meet these people I take the trouble of listening to them since they express to me their problems, their concerns and their needs, and ask me to try and do something for them.
I consider, Mr. Speaker, that the method set up by the government and which consists in increasing pensions according to the cost of living index with adjustments every three months, is not an adequate solution to stop inflation since that will not cure the economic discomforts from which everyone is suffering. All other sectors will eventually face increases, the cost of living will continue to rise, the economy will suffer more and more, and consequently there will be poverty within abundance.
Everyone knows that our governments promoted poverty, unemployment and inflation through legislative methods. So it is through opposite legislative methods that our governments will restore the national economic balance for all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, the national economic imbalance of inflation, unemployment and poverty affecting our classes of society is not accidental but indeed the result of the legislative action taken by both our Progressive Conservative and Liberal governments. Mr. Speaker, only Parliament has the right to vote legislation on the distribution of incomes and taxes among individuals, families, and corporations.
It is not the millionaire, multimillionaire, national or multinational companies or even our neighbours who have the right to vote in this Canadian Parliament but we alone, the members elected by the Canadian people. That means that we alone have the power to maintain and reestablish the national economic balance between the elements constituting our country. It is not enough to checkmate inflation, unemployment and poverty, we must above all correct this distressing situation and see to the definitive reestablishment of the national economic balance between individuals and families. In any event, the final goal of the economy can be simply reduced to the satisfaction of the population's needs. We must therefore 
work out new remedies and stimulants for our economy so as to achieve the happiness of all Canadians.
The smallest bit of our national economy must be provided with its fair share so that our quest for economic balance can be reflected in the whole of the national economy.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to emphasize that it is important to consider the present facts of our national economy as they stand because each year the difficulties of inflation, unemployment and poverty are considerably amplified despite increasing productivity and notwithstanding the clearer and clearer disorder of more and more senseless distribution.
In this very alarming situation, Mr. Speaker, we must try to identify abuses and make them disappear if we really want to solve the problems and reestablish the stability of our economy.
We of the Social Credit Party of Canada do not have a monopoly on folly. For years we have been suggesting very sensible solutions to the numerous problems of the whole world. Many members are patting their own backs and saying: "Another Social Credit illusion". But, Mr. Speaker, if we really take time out for a flashback, it is easy to see what seemed ridiculous yesterday is true today. Indeed, this government is timidly adopting measures advocated by the Social Credit Party of Canada such as increasing pensions at all levels and promising to establish a guaranteed annual income plan.
Mr. Speaker, I am fully convinced that governments will be compelled before long to apply the measures we advocate if they are really bent on taking steps to save Canada and the world from the disaster which hangs over mankind.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, it is the very high taxes and the exorbitant interest rates which are exploiting the greater part of the Canadian people and contributing to the rise in the cost of living. These exorbitant taxes and interest rates cripple the economy and create inflation, which really smother the Canadian economy and nullify the purchasing power of consumers.
We are aware that personal and corporate income taxes are under the strict jurisdiction of the elected members of Parliament whose responsibility is to meet the needs of the population as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, inflation, unemployment and poverty are the three main signs of the economic imbalance which is still hurting all economic and social levels of the Canadian people.
As I said earlier, the only way to get rid of poverty, unemployment and inflation is through restoring economic balance at the national level between individuals and families. The government of Canada alone has the power to restore quickly and thereafter maintain the kind of national balance that would eliminate inflation for the benefit of all Canadian citizens.
All this, Mr. Speaker, amply demonstrates that the time has come for a more thorough study, not only of the social security system as it applies to underprivileged citizens such as the elderly and others, but also as concerns families living on a single person's salary. I further urge the

government not to stop at this, but to undertake a study of all systems of revenues, of expenses, of hidden or secret reserves to which are entitled million- or billion-dollar companies, either national or multinational.
We suggested on various occasions that the old age security pension should be raised to $200 per month, both for single or married individuals, and to $150 in the case of the spouse of whatever age, as I indicated in my opening remarks. Mr. Speaker, like every other member, I receive on various occasions numerous requests from persons between 60 and 65. Most of the time, those people are unable to or unfit for work. I therefore urge the government once more to lower to 60 the pensionable age.
In view of the great number of people who are 60 or over, of widows and orphans without work, I most sincerely feel it is inhuman, shocking and abnormal that they be forced to live in reduced circumstances before reaching the current pensionable age of 65.
So, Mr. Speaker, I ask the government to lower the pensionable age to 60. I urge them to very seriously consider this move, I am confident it will meet with the approval of all Canadians.
