subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECT TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I enter the debate on this Creditiste motion which reads:
That this House regrets that the Government neglected to make all those who reached the age of 60, as well as their spouses although such spouses may not have reached pensionable age, eligible for the Old Age Pension.
I compliment the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) on bringing forward this important subject for debate today. The section in this motion which bothers me the most concerns allowing spouses to receive the pensions, even though they may not be 60. In some cases this is justified, but what happens in the case of a man who is considerably older than his wife, say for example, 20 or 30 years her senior? At the age of 60 he naturally qualifies for the old age pension under the proposed motion, and so does his wife.
How could this parliament justify a woman in her thirties or early forties receiving a pension, simply because her husband turned 60? This holds true if a woman is older than her spouse. The motion is too broad. In order to make it fair, we have an obligation to set up age guidelines in the case of the spouses becoming eligible for the pension when their partners turn 60.
The lowering of the age of eligibility for the old age security to 60 is a step in the right direction. It has to be done sooner or later. The increase in pressures in today's society has created a lot of premature ill-health for Canadians in the 50 to 60 age group, the very group that we are discussing. Many in this age group can no longer work, while others in the same age group cannot find work because of their age.
Whatever the situation, the present high rate of unemployment makes it virtually impossible for one spouse to find employment to compensate for whatever the other spouse would receive in old age benefits once that spouse has turned 60. For those who cannot go out and work because of illness or who cannot find employment because of their age, this adds to their hardship if their only source of income is one spouse's old age benefits.
This proposed motion would assist Canadians in those unfortunate circumstances, but nevertheless I still feel that we must place age guidelines on the spouses who are not 60, but who would automatically become eligible once their partners turned 60.
Here we have a segment of our population who, by virtue of the fact that they are classified as old age pensioners, are receiving just barely enough on which to live. We turn the coin around and see virtually millions and millions of dollars being thrown away, for example in Unemployment Insurance Commission payments and LIP grants, by which we encourage Canadians not to work. How can we justify this sort of treatment to our old age pensioners? They have been the backbone of our Canadian society for years, and now that they have reached their old age, the government of the day, in gratitude, provides them with just enough to exist on, until they are no longer a burden to the government.

Those who are new on the Canadian scene are being pampered and babied with hand-outs left and right, while those Canadians who contributed a lot of sweat, toil and tears for their country are shoved out of sight in disgrace, and are left with just enough to survive.
Ironically, Mr. Speaker, the government does not seem to realize that it is laying down a poor foundation for the very people it is babying, and creating future problems for future governments through not having enough foresight in presenting enlightened legislation which would provide adequate assitance for Canada's old age pensioners, now and in the future.
Several years ago the government had a slogan "the Just Society", and a just society it certainly created, a society more of injustice than of justice. The old age benefits fall in the area of injustices. But another area of the unjust society covers armed forces personnel living on pensions.
The government recently announced that there would be increases for those who came under the magic 85 plan in order that forces pensioners might combat inflation. Those who did not come under the magic 85 plan but who are receiving a pension were not eligible for the cost of living increases. The present set-up governing the magic 85 plan stipulates that a member of the armed forces or of the R.C.M.P. must, for example, have 30 years of service and be 55 years of age before being eligible for the special benefits under the 85 plan.
The constant reduction in the strength of the armed forces means that a lot of men in their late forties or early fifties will be pensioned off, and in many cases these men will not have enough years of service to qualify under the magic 85 plan. This certainly puts a lot of hardship on those who find obtaining employment difficult and still have a family to raise.
It seems to me that too many discriminatory policies are practised by the government. The government penalizes people because they are old or because they are in the armed forces. The policy of magic 85 is an example of discrimination. With the present cutback in the strength of the armed forces a lot of men in their late forties and early fifties will be forced out into a labour scene which cannot supply employment for them. Their pensions will be insufficient to support them and their families, and with the way the cost of living is continually rising I cannot see how they are going to make ends meet.
The government must reduce this magic 85 requirement and provide adequate increases to all armed forces personnel across the board. There is no excuse for a requirement that a man must have X number of years of service and be X number of years of age in order to qualify. This requirement does not exist in the civil service pension plans, so why should it exist for armed forces personnel? It is archaic, something out of the dark ages, and the sooner it is abolished the better for all concerned.
The most outrageous form of discrimination I have come across concerns a Mr. Builder, one of my constituents. The present Old Age Security Act does not recognize a Canadian veteran's overseas service whether or not he has resided in Canada full time after discharge. This overseas veteran was informed by the regional director of old age
December 3, 1974

security services in Victoria, "For our purposes we cannot consider you as physically present in Canada when we have confirmed that you were overseas with the Canadian Armed Forces from June 8, 1940, to March, 1946, and in addition left Canada again in November, 1946. The Old Age Security Act does not permit us to consider the overseas service as physically present in Canada for old age security."
If this is not discrimination then I must have a different interpretation of the word than the one on which the government relies. How can the government discriminate against the proud veterans who served overseas? Why should there be a difference in ruling as between one like myself, for example, who never went overseas, and one who did? If, after the war, I had gone out of the country in similar circumstances, then presumably when I came back in similar circumstances, I would qualify. Surely this is discrimination against veterans who served overseas.
Many veterans, like my constituent, did not choose to be sent overseas. If this veteran had been stationed in Canada, as I was, there would be no trouble, but he went where his country sent him, and because of this the government is penalizing him. This line of reasoning is unjust and discriminatory. There is no way in which it can be justified. Here is a case where a man's courageous war service in defence of his country is being used against him. It seems to be the policy of the government that those who have contributed nothing to the country are rewarded, while those who have contributed much to the defence and development of this great nation are penalized.

speechtext:
I cannot imagine that I am wasting my time trying to elicit new information from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). He has been in this House a long time and everything he says to me is very significant and important.

Many hon. members have taken part in today's debate which, I think, was a very good one and several have emphasized the importance of dealing with this problem as a whole. Speakers on the government side have pointed out this element and I noticed also that many hon. members from the official opposition insisted on mentioning a certain number of priorities. I note in particular the contributions made by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) and also the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes).
I would also like to thank all the Liberal members who in this debate have endeavoured most successfully to bring to our attention programs implemented over the years by the Liberal government.
With regard to the motion of the Social Credit Party of Canada, I would have appreciated it if its spokesmen had gone to more pains in order to further clarify their thoughts.	'
They talk, for instance, of optional retirement, Madam Speaker. I would like them to specify what they mean by this and how they are going to define this optional retirement. Do they include those self-employed, the farmer, the fisherman, the small businessman, the shopkeeper. How are we going to determine whether everyone has retired or not? Do my colleagues include all the wives who stay at home? Will they be considered as having voluntarily retired or not? And if they are not included, I would like the hon. members to put it on record instead of talking in quite general terms which seem very generous but are rather vague.
As to the situation that developed with respect to retirement, it is obvious that there was a tendency in the last decades to reduce the age of retirement. Even now we have pension plans in the private sector providing for retirement before the age of 65. On the other hand, one realizes that there are more people wondering about that approach. I refer particularly to the debate now taking palce in the United Stated concerning compulsory retirement at the age of 65.
More and more people in the United States are now raising the problems posed by compulsory retirement. A strong debate now going on tends to suggest that it might be preferable to reintroduce a system of optional retirement in view of the extended lifespan and productive capacity of a great many people over 65.
That debate is far from being, settled, it will be with us for a good while but, to my mind, this indicates that the situation is not irreversible, as some would like us to think.
Madam Speaker, I would like to take the few minutes remaining to me to talk about the resolution from two points of view. First, the cost aspect and, second, the priority aspect. As to the cost aspect, it will not take much time. If the proposal under consideration were simply to
[Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre).)
extend to people between the ages of 60 and 65 the benefits now available to those over 65, that would represent an amount ranging anywhere from $1.2 to $1.6 or $1.7 billions. That is new and additional money.
This is a considerable amount, although not unthinkable. I want to stress that it still represents half of all we spend at present on old age pensions and guaranteed supplements for those over 65. In fact, that amount represents roughly double the current contribution of the federal government to social assistance under the Canada Assistance Plan.
Therefore, this amount is not to be ignored and if it is provided for this purpose, it will no longer be available for other purposes. That leads me directly to the second matter I wanted to raise, that of priorities. There is no doubt that if the state were a limitless reservoir of funds, we would immediately make people at age 60 eligible for pension, and probably people at age 40, but the state is not an inexhaustible source of funds and priorities must be determined. The responsibility, the privilege, indeed the burden of government includes defining such priorities, and that applies not only to the federal government but to provincial governments as well.
So we have to make choices and make them taking into account all the requirements that now exist, all essential or useful programs in the field of social security. As an example, I will indicate some of those priorities, Madam Speaker. There is, first of all, the need to protect the income of old age pensioners facing the rise in costs. We have already escalated old age pensions with quarterly increments and I am pleased to note that as early as January 1975, these pensions will be raised again.
The basic pension to which will be added the guaranteed income supplement will be brought from $199.10 to $204.27 and, for a couple, to $389.70. The basic pension itself will be increased to $120.06 in January. With the pensions paid under the Canada Pension Plan, the maximum benefit under this plan will be raised from $109.60 to $121 per month. So a person who is now retired will receive a maximum of $241.06 under the Canada Pension Plan, including the basic pension. Those are the amounts that will become available to elderly people as of January 1975.
Things are happening in that area, and one of the priorities is to guarantee the income of those who are already retired, who are already 65, in the face of rising prices. Another priority, Madam Speaker, is more services for older people about which many hon. members talked tonight. Some of them referred to the "New Horizons" program, others to housing programs, and still others to medical care programs. Those are so many services that, of course, we must improve for our senior citizens, essential services, and there again, the government has done a great deal in the past in that area. There is still much to do and we are committed to keep on improving these services.
Another priority which does not only concern senior citizens primarily but also citizens other than those who are retired is a better income security program intended for all those who are now unable to provide for their needs. This includes a great number of physically and mentally handicapped people as well as all one parent families, especially when they are the mother's responsibility.

A fourth priority which we must take into account is the need to supplement the income of the small wage earners, those who work for a minimum wage and who have a large family, or those who have a job at minimum wage level or casual work. We must implement a program which will encourage those people to stay in the labour force and enable them to provide for their own needs and those of their families.
A fifth priority we must face is that of strengthening the essential social services such as day nurseries and programs designed to help children in general as well as programs to help juvenile delinquents and people liable to imprisonment under Canadian laws.
Another priority which was mentioned earlier by one of my colleagues is the need to provide all our citizens with moderately priced housing and there again, the opposition frequently asks the government to implement additional measures in that area.
And finally, there is the whole extremely important area of improved manpower services such as manpower training, so that welfare recipients and unemployed may reenter the labour market more easily. The problem is trying to reconcile all these priorities; I have not listed them all, but this is a series of priorities, of constant demands made upon the government. To reconcile these priorities is not only the federal government's problem; it is also of very great concern to the provinces which also have extensive responsibilities in this area.
May I remind my hon. colleagues that a very serious dispute almost arose between the provinces and the federal government when soon after my appointment we increased old age security pensions from $85 to $100 per month. I am surprised that my colleagues of the Social Credit Party of Canada who all come from Quebec have forgotten that period when the Quebec government in particular, and those of other provinces very firmly opposed unilateral action by the federal government in this field. They argued at the time that we were changing provincial priorities.
In order to achieve these goals, it is therefore essential that we maintain close co-operation with the provinces. This we endeavoured to do, Madam Speaker, as early as April 1973, and the process is now under way to review with the provinces the social security program.
This undertaking, to which we set a two-year time limit, is now nearing completion. For this reason, the federal government could not even envisage a new program or project, of the nature of that involved in the motion before us, without very seriously harming the review and being accused of bad faith by the provinces that co-operated with us in this review. May I repeat that in so doing, we would be implementing a specific provision certainly limited in nature, directed to a limited group. More importantly, it would do very little to counter poverty in this country. May I indicate once more that the intention here is to extend a universal program to a still limited group of citizens, namely the 60- to 65-year old.
What would that achieve in the fight against poverty in this country, the aim of any new undertaking in the field of social security? It would achieve very little, for the
Old Age Pensions
simple reason it would transfer funds to a great number of people who have no current need for it, because they have good jobs and they want to go on working in order to maintain their revenues.
Revenue distribution in the country according to five income groups indicates that over the last 20 years, in spite of all the social measures that were passed by governments over the last 20 years, there has been practically no change in the proportion of the income spread between the five groups in our society.
As a matter of fact, the only changes that came about affect the 40 per cent following the first 20 per cent at the top. This is the only group in which a favourable change took place. All those at the bottom level kept the same proportion they had previously and that, in spite of all the measures that were taken in the social field. It has been shown that without the present social measures, the situation of the poorest among us, namely those at the bottom level, would be twice as bad as it is now. Social measures thus help to improve their lot but in spite of that, the fact remains that income distribution in our society has practically remained the same over the last 20 years.
Now should we want a more equitable distribution of income, are we going to obtain it by extending to a limited group of citizens universal programs such as the one proposed in this motion? I do no think so. If we really want to tackle seriously this poverty problem in our society, we will have to take all available additional funds and allocate them, not in a universal way, but in a selective fashion, concentrating our attention on people who really need help. On this point, I agree with my hon. colleague from Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie), who spoke first on behalf of the Progressive Conservative Party and said we should use our funds to help those who need them the most.
And that is the general trend of the current review of social security and the fundamental priority that the government and myself have adopted.
So, what do we want to do? We want to achieve that not by considering a limited group of citizens, a single sector of the community, but by guaranteeing an income to those unable to work and earn their bread, whatever their age. We want to provide adequate help to the handicapped of 30 or 35, the chronically unemployed of 55, 56 or 57, who is unable to find work just as the chronically unemployed of 61 or 62.
And furthermore, as I was saying earlier, we want to apply available resources to supplement the income of the one who works but does not earn enough to maintain his family.
These are priorities which are not restricted to one age group, which are not restricted to a limited section of the population, to whom would be distributed universally or nearly universally funds which would benefit many people who do not need it.
These are the priorities of this government, Madam Speaker. While we have this major objective, I must once again remind hon. members that we have not ignored senior citizens.
Improvements which have been made to pensions these last few years, and especially during the last two years,

December 3, 1974
Old Age Pensions
are more important than any improvement made at any time before, and the government is rightly proud of this.
As was said earlier, we started by increasing the basic pension to $100 a month, then we geared it to the cost of living to account for inflation. These benefits were adjusted quarterly. Moreover, we made a series of very important improvements to the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan.
There was a considerable increase in the level of incomes which are subject to Canada Pension Plan contributions. We eliminated the income test for all people aged 65 to 70 under the Canada Pension Plan so that whatever their income, these people will still continue to receive a pension under the Canada Pension Plan. Moreover, as I said earlier, we fully adjusted the benefits under the Canada Pension Plan.
Madam Speaker, I hope we shall conclude our review of social security measures in the spring of 1975. At that time, I hope the provinces and the federal government will have come to an agreement about guidelines for reforming social security in Canada. As for guidelines for the future, I hope they will set priorities which will have been agreed to by the provincial and federal governments.
Again, to date, I believe we did not put aside the problems of the aged and the government does not intend to do so in the future.
Finally, we will fully discuss that question, and it is a question that I will certainly consider with my provincial counterparts. My colleagues in this House should also think about it. It is the matter I mentioned in the beginning, the possibility of optional retirement, selective retirement even at 65. I think that the debate will continue in the years ahead of us, and we will need the knowledge not only of my provincial counterparts but also of all members in this House.
Madam Speaker, once again I want to thank all members who have participated in that debate, particularly government members, for their contribution to the discussion which certainly interests all Canadian citizens. But I thought it was important to point out also to my Social Credit colleagues that we must take into account priorities when we discuss those matters and that we cannot propose such a project without referring to the whole set of other priorities which this country is now facing.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, thank you. I am glad that I am able to follow the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) because he has brought out all the old red herrings, such as that this measure would be too costly to implement, that the program to have voluntary retirement at the age of 60 would be too expensive, and so on. I hope in the course of my speech to use some of the figures that the minister used to disprove that it will be as costly as he claims. I think that the government can finance this measure.
The motion before us regrets that the government has not lowered the age of retirement to 60 so that those people can be eligible for old age security pensions. I would have used a stronger word than regret, nevertheless the NDP supports the idea of retirement at the age of 60, but we support it on a voluntary basis. We would also like to see the basic pension raised to $200 a month. I think the two are very complementary.
We have come a long way since 1926 when the House passed a measure giving the senior citizens of this country the magnificent sum of $20 at the age of 70. Hon. members reading their history will recall that this measure came into being mainly at the instigation and pressure of J. S. Woodsworth, the founder of the CCF. But it is also interesting to note that the Senate rejected that first pension plan passed in the House. Listening to the minister this evening, and to many other Liberal backbenchers, I found that they sounded very much like some of those Senators back in 1926 who said that the country could not afford an old age security pension plan. I would like to quote briefly two Senators who took part in that debate. First, Senator Donnelly, when the bill went to the upper house, said:
I feel that there is in this country many people who think they have the assurance that when they reach the age of 70, the government will provide for them, and who therefore will not make very much effort to provide for their old age. I think that in this way the Bill places a premium on extravagance and imposes a tax on thrift.
Another member, Senator Beaubien, said:
This, in my opinion, is an iniquitous measure. First of all, it is unhealthy in its basic moral principle ... If this bill passes, the obligation of the children to look after their father and mother and grandfather and grandmother goes by the board ... Is it judicious for us to impose upon our country such socialistic legislation as this-because it is nothing else-when there is no call for it?
That Senator said there was no call for pensions back in those days when workers were making 25 cents an hour.

He had one for

speechtext:
Finally by 1929 reason and humanity prevailed, and the first pension became law. Many years later, in 1972-73, when we had another minority parliament, we got a further increase in the basic pension mainly through the untiring efforts of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who, ever since coming to the House in 1942-that was one year before I was born- has been fighting for pensions for the senior citizens of this country.
In that last minority parliament, because of NDP pressure we got the basic pension up to $100 a month with a cost of living adjustment making it $117. It is now brought up to $199 with the supplement. But the situation today is not all that good because, when we look at inflation, we realize that since it is at a rate of 11 per cent pensioners still find themselves suffering hardship. Since 1961 the consumer price index has risen by 60 per cent, meaning that what $100 could buy in 1961 it now takes $160 to buy. I wonder what the minister and the government can say to the pensioner of today who, despite the increase in pensions, is falling behind because of the rapidly rising cost of living.
What does the government say about the pensioner who has eye cataracts and has to pay $107 or $110 for eye glasses? What does the government say about the pensioner who has to pay from $100 to $300 for dentures? What does the government say to pensioners who need hearing aids, which cost around $400, when we know that the cost of the components is only about $25? What does the government say to the pensioner who has seen his fuel bills increase by 31 per cent in a year? The minister says they are doing all right under the new pension increases.
What about the pensioner who has to pay outrageous prices for drugs, or the pensioner who is paying $150 or $170 a month rent or, if he owns his own home, is paying exorbitant property taxes? How do they cope? I wish the minister would follow a pensioner around the supermarket some time and see what food he buys. It is the cheapest meat, the stale food, and indeed we have heard of pensioners who have had to eat pet food. That is a disgrace in a country as wealthy as Canada, yet the minister says there is no money to increase pensions.
The fact is that 60 per cent of pensioners have an income low enough that they qualify for the guaranteed income supplement. The fact is that most of them go without proper food, clothing and accommodation. A 1972 report by economists Ross and Crawley found that about 50 per cent of Canada's aged live in poverty. I say that demonstrated a need to get the basic pension up to $200 a month.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECT TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, on a point of order, as far as I know the motion before the House is not to increase pensions but to lower the age to 60 for the same pension. I submit that the hon. member is out of order.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECT TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am arguing that the two go hand in hand. I should like to turn now to the actual business of retirement at age 60, and the minister's argument as to its cost. I think it is necessary first of all because many of our workers deserve it after having
Old Age Pensions
worked for 40 or 45 years. The life expectancy for a male in this country is 69 years, and for a female it is 76 years. That leaves the average male worker just four years to enjoy his retirement.
Lowering the retirement age to 60 would not only allow many workers to enjoy their retirement but would also allow many young people to enter the labour market, and thus help solve our unemployment problem. Many private businesses are retiring people at age 60.
The minister says that Canada has a great pension plan, but 12 other countries including France, Italy and Japan have already lowered the retirement age to 60. The minister objects to this proposed reduction. I think the ghosts of the senators are writing his speeches. For example, he is saying it is too costly, but he was saying that in 1972 when it was proposed to increase the basic pension from $82 to $100. The minority parliament changed that.
Can the government afford to reduce the pension age to 60? I think it can, for a number of reasons. The old age security income for 1972-73 was broken down as follows: personal income tax, $1,190 million, corporation tax $226 million, sales tax, $770 million. This is all applied toward pension payments. What then would it cost to reduce the pension age to 60?
The 1971 census shows 777,015 people between age 60 and 64. If we were to make retirement at age 60 voluntary I doubt whether 100 per cent of those people would elect to accept that. Studies have shown that the figure is more likely to be 30 per cent. The minister is therefore distorting things when he says it would cost between $1.2 billion and $1.6 billion. That is only if everybody retired at age 60, but if only 30 per cent did, the cost would be somewhere between $400 million and $500 million per year.
The government says it cannot afford to bring the pensionable age down to 60. I would point out to the minister that corporations are contributing $226 million to OAS. If they paid their fair share of taxes the government could easily afford it. But the minister does not want to collect extra taxes from the corporations. As of 1974 corporations have been legally able to defer paying $5.9 billion in taxes to the federal government. If the government charged 10 per cent interest on deferred taxes, which to date are interest free, it would have $500 million to contribute to bringing the pension age down to 60. So, it is quite feasible to reduce the retirement age to 60. The revenue is there, but the government is unwilling to bring in the necessary reform of the pension laws.
Canada owes her senior citizens a better deal. They built the country and we have benefited from their labour and taxes. They should be able to retire early enough to enjoy their retirement years and have an adequate income to live in dignity and security. I am sure the Liberal majority government, like the Senators in 1926, is going to deny the wishes of Canadians that the pension age be brought down to 60 and that an adequate income be provided for retirement years.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECT TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext:
At any event, I listened very carefully to the statement of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and I noted that he made some excellent comments. On the other hand, I was rather surprised to hear him mention the priorities that must come first, but it is quite normal. However, he seems to forget easily or he did not understand the stand taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) not so long ago. I have here a speech which he delivered in Granby on June 25, 1974, and in which he said, and I quote:
What was announced and what we are legislating is a coordination of the two systems so that if we are elected there will be a guaranteed annual income for all those who cannot work, whatever their age, be it 65, 60, 50, or even 20.
That was during the election period.
Of course, they were in a much better mood than after the elections.
The newspaper Le Soleil reported this on June 21, 1974:
Yesterday, Prime Minister Pierre Elliot Trudeau followed in the footsteps of Conservative Leader Robert Stanfield and announced that the old age security pension would be granted to the 60 year old spouse.
But that is what we are asking for. The text of the motion moved by my colleague for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) clearly summarizes the opinion often voiced by a great number of Canadians especially during the periods of unemployment we have known during the last years. Among the comments coming from the various speakers who took part in the discussion, it is easy to see that many understand the soundness of this motion and considering the present economic circumstances, the government should propose legislation in agreement with the request submitted.
In a brief submitted for the advancement of senior citizens in January 1965, that is almost 10 years ago, we find some interesting excerpts. After having asked for a lower eligibility age, it outlined what had happened during different periods in Canada and in many other countries of the world to legislation concerning senior citizens. I believe it would be fitting to quote certain extracts of this brief presented to the special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on the new pension plan. Once again, I am emphasizing that this brief
(Mr. Symes.]
was tabled in January 1965. Here is an extract, and I quote:
Early retirement will be compulsory in the near future thanks to automation.
Well, I can see two of them gnashing their teeth on the other side. I guess that those two are professionnal gnashers.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECT TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext: I guess they are paid for that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S NEGLECT TO PAY OLD AGE PENSION TO PERSONS AGED 60 AND THEIR SPOUSE
speechtext:
I shall continue with my quotation:
The government already recognizes age requirements by providing pension benefits to people of 65 and over, which emphasizes the difficulties older people have to face when looking for a job.
The people of the world look more and more to their governments for universal measures providing for an adequate and secure retirement. Canada is no exception and must not be.
In the United States, women of 60 and men of 65 may receive up to $200, a month; mind you, that was in 1965. In England, the age is 60 and 65; in Switzerland, 62; in New Zealand, 60; in Denmark, 62 and 67; in Soviet Union, 55 and 65. Some countries use a means test. Even in China where a few years ago old people starved to death in the streets, pensions are now paid at 50 and 55. We should be ashamed. In this vital question of age, Canada cannot lag behind that vast and overpopulated country.
It is high time a bill were passed in Canada to lower to 60 the pensionable age.
For various reasons, economic security is one of the primary needs of the aged.
It is almost ten o'clock and I would have many things to say, many details to give, many allusions to make and facts to tell about the minister's visit to the riding of Kamouraska and to a home for the aged where he must have noted that most of the time the aged never get their increase. Federal-provincial relations should be greatly improved so that the increased granted to senior citizens are not retained by provincial governments under the pretense that maintenance costs increase with the cost of living.
A real pension plan should be designed to enable older people to use their maturity at this important stage of their life, which would allow them to put into practice a philosophy of life impossible to attain at an earlier age.
While their declining physical strength or the disappearance of friends may have closed some doors to them, their maturity opens others. The disappointments of life has often increased their wisdom so that they can avoid trouble. Whatever privileges the retired must give up he still has the right to usefulness and the right to dignity.
The Economic Council of Canada states that over 700,000 Canadians among elder people live below the poverty line. Keep on laughing you two sneerers from Sherbrooke! How does the Economic Council of Canada define poverty? That is not happening elsewhere, it is happening in Canada.
At page 104 of the Fifth Annual Review of the Economic Council of Canada released in September 1968, one reads, and I quote:
To feel poverty is, among other things, to feel oneself an unwilling outsider-a virtual nonparticipant in the society in which one lives.
December 3, 1974

The problem of poverty in developed industrial societies is increasingly viewed not as a sheer lack of essentials to sustain life, but as an insufficient access to certain goods, services, and conditions of life which are available to everyone else and have come to be accepted as basic to a decent, minimum standard of living.
Those are valid reasons that should prompt the government to pass legislation aimed at guaranteeing a minimum level of income and security for people of 60.
We should not wait for all sorts of manifestations to happen to pass legislation providing older people with a suitable pension at the age of 60.
Legislation should also be geared toward creating a climate of security for older people so they can have some compensation for the years of hardships and economic distress that too many poor, particularly in our stupid system of today, had to suffer in a country as rich as ours. Society is not fulfilling all its obligations if all it does is look after the material well-being of the retired, without considering their emotional and psychological needs. It is a mistake to think that we can somehow send older people to the pasture by providing them with food, clothing and shelter.
Canada must try to make full use of the huge tank of ideas, skills and competence represented by its million and a half inhabitants over the age of 60.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-CANADA-CUBA ROUTE-POSSIBLE COMPLETION OF NEGOTIATIONS
AIR TRANSPORT-CANADA-CUBA ROUTE-POSSIBLE COMPLETION OF NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on October 16 I raised with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) the question of completing negotiations for regular passenger service between Cuba and Canada. I was a little surprised at the minister's reply which seemed to indicate a lack of progress in this important matter. I had thought that after so long a period of discussion our two countries were closer to formal agreement.
As many in this House know, I have long been an advocate of closer trade and contact with the Caribbean area and in that area Cuba is an important, indeed very important, element. In 1971 it was my pleasure, along with the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart) and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), to visit Cuba. I think we were the first group of Canadian parliamentarians to make an official visit to that island. There is a great potential for growth in that beautiful island, and their economic efforts merit great commendation. For those who denigrate the Castro regime, I suggest they recall or research the kind of Cuban society, the kind of Cuban government which preceded the present system of political organization.
One of the strong moves on the international scene by the government led by the right hon. gentleman from

December 3, 1974
Adjournment Debate
Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) dealt with Cuba. In 1962, when Washington inspired a hemispheric embargo of Cuba, the Canadian government decided to retain diplomatic and commercial ties with Havana. We kept the doors open, but for a long time I think we have not moved sufficiently through those open doors.
Of late, things have improved. There has been a welcome increase in trade between Cuba and Canada. Our foreign trade with Cuba, $58.8 million in 1971, was practically the same in 1972 but rose to $81.9 million for 1973 with excellent prospects for 1974. Looking at the import side we see that the balance is decidedly in Canada's favour.
One thing which impressed me when I was in Cuba was the large number of trade delegations seeking to make stronger commercial contacts with the republic. I saw many European businessmen there and many Japanese but few, too few, Canadians. The Cubans, with a pragmatism which characterizes their system, have a division of their Trade and Commerce designated as "Trade with Capitalist Countries".
The opportunities for increasing trade with Cuba are encouraging and I welcome signs of leadership from both the south and the north. A few months ago the Cubans bought a shipload of first class hogs from Prince Edward Island; we have also done much in contributing to the Cuban development of pure-bred cattle of exceptional quality. An enterprising young businessman from Charlottetown has sold several orders of equipment which has done much to improve the efficiency of Cuban fish processing plants.
The Atlantic provinces' chambers of commerce plan a visit to Cuba. This is a welcome and worthwhile move. In the development of closer ties between businessmen and people generally, the provision of comfortable, convenient, regular passenger air service is very much of the essence. I should like to see a direct Halifax-Havana service or a direct Charlottetown-Havana service, but would settle for Montreal or Toronto. There is need for an upgrading of priorities in connection with this matter.
The economic realities today dictate and underline the urgency of diversifying our trade patterns. New markets are essential. We must develop them. Trade and commerce on the Atlantic seaboard by sea and air should be encouraged. I renew my appeal for increased celerity and concern with regard to this important area of transportation improvement. If the parliamentary secretary, my fellow islander, can announce tonight that arrangements are moving very fast, if he can give a date for the inaugural flight and arrange for both of us to be on it, my cup of joy will be full indeed.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-CANADA-CUBA ROUTE-POSSIBLE COMPLETION OF NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
As the President of Privy Council (Mr. Sharp), the House leader, pointed out at the time, Madam Speaker, the government is not at present engaged in any "air negotiations" with Cuba. However, recent development in Canada-Cuba relations may well lead to such negotiations in the foreseeable future.
It has been recognized for some time that there is need to provide direct air connections between the two countries. There have been serious delays in communication,
|Mr. Macquarrie.]
and in the handling of mail and freight to Cuba through the Mexican postal administration. It was proposed at one time that Cubana Airlines might operate charter flights to Montreal for the carriage of freight and mail only, at more or less regular intervals provided such traffic were shared by a Canadian carrier, but Cubana did not actively pursue this type of operation.
Canada's trade with Cuba has expanded considerably since 1970-71, as the hon. member has pointed out. While the volume of air passenger traffic between the two countries has not been particularly large, tourist traffic from Canada appears to be increasing. Air Canada has been associated with inclusive tour charters to Havana, but until recently had shown little interest in starting a regular service.
During 1973, 5,000 or more Canadians arrived in Cuba, on charter flights using Air Canada equipment. Cuban autorities, of course, along with the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie), would like to see that figure expanded. I think the hon. member will be interested to know that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) will be recommending shortly to his cabinet colleagues that we enter into negotiations to work out a bilateral air agreement with Cuba.

subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE JAMES BAY SETTLEMENT NOT USED AS GUIDE IN SETTLING LAND CLAIMS OF OTHER NATIVE GROUPS
INDIAN AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE JAMES BAY SETTLEMENT NOT USED AS GUIDE IN SETTLING LAND CLAIMS OF OTHER NATIVE GROUPS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to refer to a question I put to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan) on November 18. The question related to a statement the minister had made on regarding the James Bay settlement as a precedent. I am happy to see the minister here tonight, since this is an important question and one in which many people across Canada are extremely interested.
I shall not take up much time, since the question itself is very basic-as a matter of fact it could be answered by a brief yes or no, although I hope the minister will be disposed to give the House a more elaborate reply.
I should like to ask the minister whether he can state that the government of Canada is prepared to negotiate native claims in the Northwest Territories in good faith, and without any preconceived limits or constraints arising from the James Bay settlement or other settlements? The reason I ask this question is that I am of the opinion that many people are afraid that that settlement will be used as a model, or formula. We agree that the settlement is good inasmuch as it was negotiated; and secondly the government of Canada admitted that the native peoples of this country do have aboriginal claims in certain areas. Basically that is the question I should like the minister to elaborate on at this time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Judd Buchanan (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE JAMES BAY SETTLEMENT NOT USED AS GUIDE IN SETTLING LAND CLAIMS OF OTHER NATIVE GROUPS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, since the agreement in principle on a land settlement between the province of Quebec and the James Bay Cree Indians and Inuit of northern Quebec was announced, concern has
December 3, 1974

been expressed by other native groups who are preparing their land claims that the Quebec agreement would form a rigid basis for all future land settlements. Recent comments in the press may have contributed to this concern.
It is my view as the minister most directly involved with native claims that the James Bay settlement is an immensely important historical event, not only for the native peoples of James Bay but for all native peoples of Canada, simply because the settlement resulted from a process of negotiations. This is the process established by the government's major policy statement of August 8, 1973, and I believe the settlement indicates clearly the success of this policy. As a process, the settlement will obviously have a bearing on native claims negotiated elsewhere in Canada.
However, again I wish to emphasize that each individual claim will be considered on its merits, and that the importance of regional differences as they appear in each claim will be recognized. It is not a rigid formula. For these reasons, a different pattern of settlement from that of James Bay will likely emerge after separate negotiations with the various native groups involved in each area. We are prepared to negotiate in good faith on this basis, realizing that there will be differing conditions and aspirations, as well as different requirements in each region of the country.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-DATE OF INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION ESTABLISHING INDEPENDENT ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION BOARD
BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-DATE OF INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION ESTABLISHING INDEPENDENT ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION BOARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, at the end of October an airplane owned by PanArctic Oils Limited of Calgary crashed through the sea ice in the far north. Thirty-two people died, and two survived the accident. I was interested in it, as I am sure many Canadians were, because of the very extensive loss of life, yet in these days what at one time would have held the attention of the world for a long period becomes the current day's interest, and seems to disappear without further mention in a very short space of time.
As I say, there were a couple of survivors from the accident and the airplane almost made it to its destination. Under those circumstances especially I think questions are raised as to whether every precaution was taken in terms of safety, and in terms of checks and inspections of the plane itself.
Subsequent to the crash I received a letter from a constituent in which several questions were raised as to the sort of safety inspection done on privately owned planes as well as that required for commercial flights. Any plane carrying as large a number of passengers and crew as this, bears with it on every trip people whose services would be of considerable value to a large section of the population who depend upon them.
I asked a question about bringing forward in the House the proposed independent accident investigation board that was promised in the Speech from the Throne. At that time I had two supplementary questions which were more
Adjournment Debate
specific that I wished to direct to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand). At this time I should like to direct them to the parliamentary secretary.
Can the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mclsaac) give an indication concerning what investigative procedures are now underway in regard to this accident? Also can he say, when the promised independent accident investigation board is set up, whether this particular accident will be referred to it? I realize this would be somewhat retroactive. However, considering the very large loss of life I think this is the sort of accident which should be thoroughly investigated by as impartial as possible an investigative body. The families and friends of those killed and injured, as well as a great many other people involved in this sort of flight in the far north, will be very interested in the reply from the minister.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cliff Mclsaac (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-DATE OF INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION ESTABLISHING INDEPENDENT ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION BOARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in reply to the hon. member may I say I shall have to answer the latter part of this question at a later time as I do not have the facts with me tonight to deal with it.
In respect of the question as first presented, in the Speech from the Throne, as the hon. member mentioned correctly, the government did state its intention that an independent transportation accident investigation body would be established by parliament. This proposal is based on a report made to the ministry of transport by General H. A. MacLean, who studied present Canadian federal organizations for the investigation of transportation accidents and the promotion of transportation safety.
The proposals for the new transportation accident investigation body would include the investigation of aircraft accidents, railway accidents and marine accidents. This would involve not only a new act of parliament to set up such a body; it would also involve amendments to the Aeronautics Act, the Railway Act, the Canada Shipping Act and other legislation dealing with these matters.
At the present time the proposals for the new independent transportation accident investigation body are being studied by senior officials of the ministry of transport. It is anticipated that recommendations in respect of specific legislation will be going forward through Cabinet, to the Department of Justice, to prepare all necessary legislation in consultation with officers of the ministry of transport in the very near future.
I am confident the hon. member will agree that in the meantime we must make sure that the means now at our disposal, which have served us well in the past to investigate accidents such as the one to which he referred, will continue to be as responsive as possible to the needs of the

December 3, 1974
Canadian public. With regard to when the hon. member can expect to see the new legislation, may I say I am not able to tell him specifically the date but certainly it will be
sometime during the current session after the Christmas recess.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.20 p.m.
